visits.text: Alkmaar's cheese market (Kaasmarkt) takes place every Friday morning, from the last Friday in March to the last Friday in September, from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. on the Waagplein. The cheese carriers' guild has existed since 1593: you will see carts loaded with wheels of Gouda, ritualized negotiations and the weighing at the Waag. It is the oldest and most famous cheese market in the Netherlands.
The Hollands Kaasmuseum is housed in Alkmaar's former Waag (weigh house), a 14th-century building. It traces the history of the cheese trade in the region from the Middle Ages to the present day.

Alkmaar's historic center can be explored on foot along its canals: gabled houses, pedestrian streets, and the atmosphere of a well-preserved small provincial Dutch town. Allow 45 minutes for a complete circuit.

activities.text: Rent a bike and cycle through Zuid-Kennemerland National Park: wooded dunes, semi-wild Konik horses and trails toward Bloemendaal beach. Allow for a day trip from Alkmaar.

visits.text: White surfaces, glass, and slender steel columns: De Kunstlinie, now called KAF, seems to float weightlessly at the edge of the Weerwater. The Japanese firm SANAA designed and built it between 2000 and 2006; three performance halls rise from an almost square base punctuated by courtyards. If the lobby is open, look for Michael Lin’s large mural, then follow the Esplanade toward The Wave.

Completed in 2005, René van Zuuk’s The Wave undulates above the Weerwater like a swell frozen in place. Its gray-green facade is a reminder that you are walking on a former seabed. Its neighbors, Side by Side and Silverline, complete this waterfront, which grew out of the downtown plan launched in 1994 in the spirit of Rem Koolhaas’s firm OMA. These are residential buildings: admire them from the quay.

The Groene Kathedraal follows the floor plan of Notre-Dame de Reims with 178 Lombardy poplars, planted on April 16, 1987, by artist Marinus Boezem. Measuring about 150 m by 75 m, with trunks around thirty meters tall serving as pillars, this is a nave that grows rather than being built. Nearby, a clearing cut into a young beech grove outlines the same cathedral. Allow 1 hour for both, then head north toward the Oostvaardersplassen.

activities.text: A planned new town, Almere is far from a bland suburb: its first house dates to 1976, and its downtown reads like an architecture catalog. The tourist office’s architecture walk covers a 4.8 km loop in 1 hour 30 minutes, starting at the VVV Almere Citystore. Look up at De Citadel, where Christian de Portzamparc placed homes on the rooftops of stores, then step inside De Nieuwe Bibliotheek, which opened in 2010 and was designed like a department store.

days_plan.itin_title: Flevoland in 3 Days: Polders, Marker Wadden, and Urk

visits.text: The red-and-white Bornrif lighthouse at Hollum has watched over the coast since 1880 and is one of the few Wadden island lighthouses you can climb. 236 steps take you to a height of 55 m, with views of Terschelling and Schiermonnikoog in good weather. Adult admission around €4.75.

The Abraham Fock Museum chronicles sea rescues organized from Ameland for generations. The distinctive local feature: rescuers used horses to launch the lifeboats—a full-scale demonstration takes place regularly in the village of Hollum. Check the calendar before arriving.

In the 't Oerd reserve, spoonbills fly over the dunes in tight formation in late afternoon. This ancient dune system in the island's east shelters harriers and mergansers. Accessible on foot or by bike from Buren; marked trails.

18th-century shipowner-captains left their houses in the villages of Hollum, Ballum, and Nes—painted gabled facades, carved lintels, gardens enclosed by brick walls. These “commandeurswoningen” are listed as heritage. An interpretive panel in front of each house traces the owner's story.

activities.text: Cycle from Nes to Hollum along the shell paths, with the sea wind in your face or at your back, depending on your luck. Standard and electric bikes are available to rent at the ferry landing in Nes. The cycle paths avoid the roads and run alongside the dunes.

If the tide is low, join a wadlopen excursion organized by Expeditie Waddenzee: walking on the Wadden Sea floor—a UNESCO area since 2009—toward sandbanks with seals is a strange experience. Excursions from Hollum or Nes, with a mandatory guide.

Each month, the Abraham Fock Museum organizes a demonstration of launching a horse-drawn lifeboat—a technique unique in the world that saved lives for decades. Check the date on the island's website before your stay.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Netherlands: Wadden, Friesland & Groningen in 13 days

visits.text: Amsterdam's Canal Ring (Grachtengordel) has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2010: three concentric canals dug in the 17th century, lined with 1,500 gabled houses. Stroll along the Herengracht, the most elegant, to understand why Amsterdam was the world's commercial capital during the VOC era.

The Jordaan was a working-class neighborhood in the 17th century—today it's Amsterdam's most sought-after district. Its narrow lanes, flower-draped bridges, and quintessentially Dutch brown cafés deserve an hour of aimless wandering.

The Rijksmuseum houses over 8,000 objects spanning 800 years of Dutch history, including Rembrandt's The Night Watch (3.6 m × 4.4 m) and Vermeer's The Milkmaid. The neo-Gothic building was designed by Pierre Cuypers and opened in 1885. Book your ticket online: time slots fill up fast.

Zaanse Schans is a living museum village 20 minutes north of Amsterdam, where green wooden houses and 17th- and 18th-century windmills have been gathered since 1961. Entry to the village is free—only the windmills and certain workshops charge admission. Arrive on a weekday before 10 a.m. to experience the atmosphere without the crowds.

You can visit several working windmills: De Kat produces pigments for dyes, De Zoeker has pressed oil since 1610, and Het Jonge Schaap is a sawmill. Climb onto a windmill's gallery for the best view over the Zaan River.

The Negen Straatjes (Nine Streets) form a grid of lanes perpendicular to the canals in the Jordaan. Vintage boutiques, concept stores, and independent cafés share these nine little streets: this is where Amsterdammers do their shopping.

The Van Gogh Museum holds the world's largest collection of the artist's works: over 200 paintings, 500 drawings, and 700 letters. Don't miss Sunflowers, The Bedroom, and The Potato Eaters. Booking online is essential—tickets often sell out two weeks in advance.

Vondelpark is Amsterdam's green lung: 47 hectares of lawns, ponds, and outdoor stages five minutes from the Museum Quarter. In summer, free concerts take place in the evenings. It's the perfect spot to catch your breath between museums.

Amsterdam-Noord is reached by free ferry from behind Centraal Station; take the one that serves NDSM. The former NDSM shipyard is home to bars, artists' studios and monumental street art. A side of Amsterdam that tourists in a hurry never see.

activities.text: A canal cruise departing from Centraal Station is the best way to grasp Amsterdam's 17th-century fan-shaped urban plan. From the deck, you'll see the leaning houses and the city's 1,500 bridges from an angle impossible to capture on foot. Allow 1 hour and 15 minutes.

Rent a bike and pedal through the Jordaan to the Brouwersgracht—considered Amsterdam's most photogenic canal. Early morning, before 9 a.m., it's almost deserted. Bikes can be rented everywhere near Centraal in minutes.

The workshops at Zaanse Schans offer continuous demonstrations: wooden clog making (you'll see the carving machine in action), artisanal cheese-making with tastings, and traditional baking. Plan on an hour to visit several.

The Waterlooplein flea market is open every day except Sunday, and the Albert Cuyp Market, open since 1905, is the Netherlands' largest street market. Both are less than 20 minutes' walk from the Rijksmuseum—choose one to conclude your stay.

visits.text: Built between 1684 and 1686, Paleis Het Loo was the residence of the House of Orange-Nassau until 1962 before becoming a national museum. It reopened in 2023 after major renovations, and entry is now via an underground passage beneath a glass roof that lets the light through. The Baroque gardens, designed according to the vision of William III and Mary II, have been restored to their original state. Closed Mondays; adult ticket around €21.

The Baroque gardens are impeccable: they were designed by Claude Desgots, Le Nôtre's nephew, to impress royal visitors. Symmetrical parterres, fountains and sculpted hedges recreate the 17th-century state. In spring, the flowering is particularly spectacular. Allow at least an hour just for the gardens.

activities.text: Stop by the royal stables to see the exhibition of carriages and ceremonial vehicles. The space is less visited than the palace apartments and offers a striking contrast between the splendour of 18th-century coaches and the royal family's first automobiles. Count on 30 to 40 minutes.

visits.text: Stand on the Vlintenbrug or Vrouwenbrug to see Appingedam’s hanging kitchens, wooden kitchens projecting over the Damsterdiep. The warehouses along the quay became homes, and their residents gained space by suspending these additions above the water. Continue through the narrow streets of the only town in the province besides Groningen to hold medieval city rights, granted in 1327.

Saints in faded colors watch over the vaults of the Nicolaïkerk: Mary on her crescent moon, Saint Nicholas wearing his miter, and the Four Crowned Saints, patrons of builders. Whitewashed after the Reformation, these paintings were uncovered during restoration from 1948 to 1954, in a church built in stages from around 1200 to 1560. The organ renovated by Hinsz in 1744 is still used for recitals: check visiting hours before coming.

days_plan.itin_title: Groningen in 3 Days: Wadden Mudflat Walks, Seals, and a Fortress

visits.text: The costumed actors at the Nederlands Openluchtmuseum truly inhabit their roles: brewer, blacksmith, tram driver. This 44-hectare open-air museum in Arnhem relocates authentic buildings from every region of the Netherlands and fills them with characters who talk about the past in the present tense. Allow a full day. The Museum Pass is accepted.

Arnhem deserves better than its reputation as the “city of the bridge too far”. Its Sonsbeek Park, right in the centre, hosts contemporary sculptures scattered across terraced lawns overlooking the town. The park is entirely free and little visited by foreign tourists—a real breath of fresh air.

In Sonsbeek Park, sculptures emerge from the morning mist among old beeches. The park dates from the 19th century and its landscape design makes it one of Gelderland's finest urban parks. It connects the Openluchtmuseum to Arnhem's city centre on foot in a pleasant hour's walk.

activities.text: If you visit on a weekday, the Openluchtmuseum is much less crowded than on weekends: the actors have more time for visitors and the interactive workshops are less busy. Allow at least three hours to see the brewery, windmill, farm and historic tram sections. The tram makes a circuit of the site.

At the John Frost Bridge, a plaque commemorates the battle of September 1944. Walking across takes ten minutes, and the view of the Arnhem skyline is the best in the city. The Airborne Museum at Hartenstein, in Oosterbeek, is the leading museum on Operation Market Garden if you want to learn more.

visits.text: Enjoy the award-winning beach of Bergen aan Zee, honored eight times with the Blue Flag for its exemplary cleanliness and safety. This seaside resort founded specifically as a holiday destination attracts thousands of visitors each year seeking pristine nature and fresh North Sea air.

activities.text: Try your hand at water sports on this coast renowned for its ideal conditions. Kitesurfing and sailing are practiced here in an exceptional setting, with schools offering lessons for all levels, from beginners to experienced participants.

Stroll along the long stretch of fine sand where the North Sea laps at the shore. The infinite horizon and preserved dunes create a soothing landscape, perfect for long invigorating walks to the sound of the waves.

visits.text: On the Brabant side, Biesbosch MuseumEiland in Werkendam is a starting point for exploring the park. Its pavilions tell the story of this freshwater delta’s formation after the St. Elizabeth’s Flood in 1421 and the work of tending willow beds, cut every three years. You can climb the planted roof to a lookout point. Bring a bank card: it is the only accepted payment method.

activities.text: You’ll glide silently through the creeks of the Biesbosch aboard the fluisterboot, the “whisper boat” departing from MuseumEiland. The cruise lasts 75 minutes and includes museum admission: €23.50 per adult. Beavers, reintroduced starting in 1988, inhabit the park; spotting them takes luck. Book your place online before coming; for a same-day departure, call the museum.

De Pannekoek, MuseumEiland’s open-air museum, covers 8 hectares of coppiced willows, roughly ten soccer fields. A marked 2 km loop passes a willow garden and the funnel of a former duck decoy, a traditional duck trap. Walk it after the cruise, wearing shoes that can handle mud.

days_plan.itin_title: Western Brabant in 3 Days: Breda, Biesbosch and Heusden

visits.text: Four centuries after its construction between 1614 and 1617, Bolsward’s Renaissance Stadhuis became home to the De Tiid center in 2021, inaugurated by King Willem-Alexander. You can visit the wood-paneled council chamber, the restored tower, and an exhibition on Titus Brandsma, who was born near the city and canonized in 2022. Open Monday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and Sunday from noon.

The carved choir stalls of the Martinikerk, ranked among the finest in the Netherlands, alone make Bolsward worth a stop. Consecrated in 1459, the church preserves wall paintings from around 1475, a pulpit from 1662 supported by two eagles, and a Hinsz organ with 3,186 pipes, first played in 1781. Ask for opening hours at De Tiid, which houses the tourist office.

A glass roof rests on ruined walls: the Broerekerk, the church of a 13th-century Franciscan friary, burned on May 8, 1980, and remains a roofed ruin. In front, Johan Creten’s dark bat spouts water like a cathedral gargoyle. Climb the steps on its back, as the artwork invites you to do: children can play on it safely.

days_plan.itin_title: Eleven Cities of Friesland in 5 Days, Along the Elfsteden Route

visits.text: The Netherlands' largest hunebed, D27, measures 22.5 m long and dates back some 5,000 years. The stones, transported from Scandinavia by glaciers, weigh up to 20 tonnes apiece. The Hunebedcentrum, right next door, tells how the first Funnelbeaker culture farmers erected them. Older than the pyramids.

In the Oertijdpark, the scent of a wood fire accompanies the reconstruction of an open-air Neolithic village. “Prehistoric men” in period costume demonstrate flint-working and cooking. Open for demonstrations only during Dutch school holidays.

activities.text: Follow the Hondsrug trails to other hunebeds scattered across the heath: 54 remain in total in Drenthe. Hondsrug Geopark panels guide you through 150,000 years of glacial landscape. The Hunebedcentrum provides hiking maps.

visits.text: Once a refuge for shipwreck survivors, now a lookout: the Drenkelingenhuisje stands on stilts at the edge of the beach on the Boschplaat side. Approved in 1865, the hut sheltered survivors who made it out of the surf; a storm destroyed it on February 16, 1962, and it was rebuilt in 2000 near Paal 25. Climb the stairs for a view of the North Sea: it remains accessible year-round.

activities.text: The true Dutch end of the world begins at the Boschplaat, an uninhabited nature reserve covering nearly half of Terschelling. Some 60 to 65 bird species nest across approximately 4,400 hectares of salt marshes, dunes, and mudflats, including around 200 pairs of spoonbills. Leave your bike at the Paal 19 parking area, then follow the sandy path at the foot of the dunes on foot or by bike: the eastern tip is 8 km from the entrance.

days_plan.itin_title: Terschelling and Harlingen in 3 Days, Bound for the Wadden

visits.text: Leave your car in the free parking lot at the information center, then walk five to ten minutes to Bourtange fortress, a pentagon surrounded by moats. Reconstructed as it stood in 1742 through a project begun in the 1960s and completed in 1992, it can be explored along its ramparts in 30 minutes, with bastions and ravelins below your feet. Since the village is inhabited, admission is free year-round; finish on the Marktplein beneath its linden trees.

The only road between Germany and Groningen passed through here: Bourtange fortress, completed in 1593 to block it, held out against the Prince-Bishop of Münster in 1672. Its museums tell the story of garrison life and the village’s Jewish history, in a synagogue that the tourist office describes as the only well-preserved one along the German-Dutch border. Book the combined ticket online, valid for a two-hour time slot; during the season, opening hours are generally 11 AM to 4:30 PM.

days_plan.itin_title: Groningen in 3 Days: Wadden Mudflat Walks, Seals, and a Fortress

visits.text: In our view, the Grote Kerk alone makes Breda worth a stop. Its 97-meter tower, built between 1468 and 1509, rises above the Grote Markt and the Brabantine Gothic nave. In the Prinsenkapel, the mausoleum of the Nassau-Breda family, ancestors of the royal family, the vaults painted in 1533 by Raphael’s pupil Tommaso Vincidor have regained their colors. Also look for the mummified 15th-century cat discovered inside the walls in 1906 and named Polleke in 2025. The exterior restoration officially ends in February 2027: some scaffolding may still obscure the choir.

Great legend, wrong address: the Spanjaardsgat, the water gate of Kasteel van Breda, is not where the peat boat brought in its 68 hidden soldiers in 1590. According to the VisitBreda tourist office, the action took place elsewhere; the gate, built some twenty years later between the Granaattoren and the Duiventoren, keeps its memory alive. The castle has housed the Royal Military Academy since 1826. The interior can only be visited with the VVV, on the last Saturday of the month and during school breaks; valid ID is required.

Garden herbs scent the courtyard of Breda’s Begijnhof, just steps from the bustle of Catharinastraat. Founded in 1267 and located here since 1535, the beguinage has 29 houses arranged around a garden of more than 300 herbs, restored in 1970. The last beguine, Sister Frijters, died in 1990, but women living alone still reside here. Visit between noon and 6 p.m., when the courtyard is open, and keep your voice down: these are people’s homes.

You’ll cross Park Valkenberg between the station and the center: the former garden of Kasteel van Breda became a public park in 1886. The Willemstraat entrance leads past the Baroniemonument, designed by P.J.H. Cuypers in 1905; another gate opens beside the Begijnhof. Look for John Körmeling’s ’t T Huis, an almost transparent pavilion whose facade displays drinks, most of which are not for sale. Save the park for a break between visits.

William the Silent and Anna van Egmont lived at Kasteel van Breda, and this dynasty comes to life at the Stedelijk Museum Breda. The permanent multimedia exhibition “The Nassaus of Breda” connects the city’s history with that of the House of Orange-Nassau. The museum on Boschstraat also showcases artists associated with Breda, such as Ruud van Empel and Sef Peeters. Allow 1 hour 15 minutes; the Dutch museum card (Museumkaart) is accepted. Closed Mondays.

activities.text: If you’re over 12 and have the stamina for 287 steps, climb the Grote Kerk tower with a guide. The climb takes about 1 hour and leads through narrow passages before emerging above Breda’s rooftops. The current spire dates from 1702, following the fire of 1694. Book your time slot through the church’s online ticket office: €10 for a standard ticket, €7.50 for ages 12–18 and students. Bring binoculars on a clear day.

Breda’s harbor has come a long way: filled in in 1965, it made way for a road with the Netherlands’ first underground parking garage beneath it. Excavated again, it reopened on the last weekend of June 2007 and once more welcomes boats. Board at the De Thor ticket boat for 1 hour on the singels, the city’s canals: cruises run from April to October, with schedules varying by month and final departures before closing time. Outside the season, simply follow the quays to the Spanjaardsgat.

places.name: Broek In Waterland

visits.text: Discover Broek in Waterland, a picturesque village of colorful wooden houses that seems frozen in time. This authentic 17th-century gem, located just a few kilometers from Amsterdam, offers total immersion in traditional Holland with its peaceful canals and bucolic atmosphere untouched by mass tourism.

activities.text: Wander along the canals lined with historic houses featuring pastel facades and admire the typically Dutch architecture of this heritage-listed village. The reflections of old houses in the calm water create a postcard-perfect setting ideal for photography enthusiasts.

visits.text: Officially a city of 170 inhabitants: the sign says “stadsgrens”—city limits—after just a few dozen metres. Bronkhorst received its city rights in 1482 and has never grown beyond its medieval core since. Red-brick houses with decorated façades line three main streets; a complete walk takes under twenty minutes. It's the kind of place you want to see before the “Instagram spot” signs appear.

Bronkhorst's chapel dates from 1344 and was once the private chapel of the castle of the lords of Bronckhorst. All that remains of the castle is the Slotheuvel, a castle mound visible on the way out of the village. The chapel now serves as a cultural centre with occasional exhibitions. It's the only standing medieval monument in Bronkhorst; its bell tower is visible from every point in the village.

activities.text: Take the little cable ferry across the IJssel to Brummen — a few minutes' crossing, a few euros. It's one of the few ferry links still operating on this stretch of river. On the other side, a short walk leads to the first IJssel levees with a view of Bronkhorst from the water.

visits.text: Too large for this small harbor town? Brouwershaven’s Sint-Nicolaaskerk gives that impression as soon as you reach the forecourt. Its scale and Renaissance organ case recall a history more ambitious than the present-day town suggests. Interior access depends on opening times and events; plan primarily to explore the exterior, without counting on it always being open.

Brouwershaven’s harbor reaches almost to the tables in the town center, with the Stadhuis as a backdrop. The former town hall took on a new use after the municipal reorganization; its Renaissance facade stands out on the square. Look for the statue of Justice above the door; the town hall’s interior is closed to the public.

days_plan.itin_title: Zeeland in 4 Days: Harbors, Beaches, and the Dike Route

places.name: Buren

visits.text: In 1551, William of Orange married Countess Anna van Egmont in Buren. Both were 18 at the time. The Museum Buren & Oranje, housed in the former town hall on the Markt, tells the story of this connection between the small town and the Dutch royal family. Thanks to this marriage, the monarch of the Netherlands still holds the title of Count of Buren. From April through October, the museum is open on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Saturdays from 10:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and on Thursdays from 1 p.m.

The Koninklijk Weeshuis, Buren’s royal orphanage, was founded in 1612 by Maria of Nassau, daughter of William of Orange and Anna van Egmont. On the garden gate, three statues represent Faith, Hope, and Charity. The building is not open to visitors: look at its long Renaissance facade from the street. A short walk away, the Sint-Lambertuskerk is the church where the princely couple married. Maria is buried beneath its chancel. The church is generally open from April through September, Tuesday through Saturday, and admission is free.

activities.text: Then walk around Buren’s old town: the center is small, and 30 minutes is enough. Pass through the Culemborgse Poort, built around 1400, the only city gate still standing. Continue to De Prins van Oranje, a stone grain mill built in 1716 that still operates. The mill is mainly open to visitors on Saturday and Sunday afternoons, as well as Wednesday afternoons during the tourist season.

visits.text: Every evening at 9:55 p.m., a bell still rings in the Binnenpoort, Culemborg’s “inner gate.” This ringing, known as the papklok, once warned residents that the city gates would close at 10 p.m. The gate tower dates from the 14th century, and an extra story was added in 1557. It is the only one of the city’s seven gates still standing. Pass beneath its archway to reach the Markt, the main square.

The Stadhuis, Culemborg’s town hall, stands on the Markt with its tall Gothic facade and stepped gables. It was built between 1534 and 1539 to designs by architect Rombout Keldermans. Elisabeth of Culemborg, the town’s last sovereign ruler, commissioned it. Culemborg is also the birthplace of Jan van Riebeeck, born in 1619. In 1652, he founded the fort in South Africa from which Cape Town developed. For a photo, step back to the center of the square.

If you’re traveling with children, the Elisabeth Weeshuis Museum will appeal to them more than a traditional museum. This former orphanage was built in 1560 with the inheritance of Elisabeth of Culemborg, who died childless. A visit brings the orphans’ daily routines to life, including their strict schedules, rules, and punishments. A small section of the medieval rampart survives behind the building. The museum is open Wednesday through Sunday, from noon to 5 p.m.: arrive before 4 p.m. to allow enough time.

visits.text: Around 1830, Jan David Zocher redesigned the park at Kasteel Twickel and had the orangery built there; Hugo Poortman added the surrounding formal garden in the late 19th century, and the last baroness created a rock garden. The castle, still inhabited, opens only a few days a year; the gardens charge admission and can be visited from April to October, Wednesday through Sunday.

Peaceful on the surface, the lands of Twickel conceal a valuable resource underground: salt was discovered here in 1886. In Delden’s historic center, the Zoutmuseum traces this mineral from its discovery through production to its uses today. Save it for late afternoon: it opens only from 2 to 5 p.m. and is closed on Tuesdays.

The Oude Blasiuskerk predates Delden: a manuscript mentions it as early as 1119. Construction of its tower began in 1516 but stopped at two levels, and the absence of belfry louvers reveals that a third story was never built. Restoration work between 1965 and 1968 uncovered murals beneath the plaster; ask at the tourist information office about visiting the interior.

activities.text: You can explore Delden’s streets by following Kunststappen, an outdoor art trail whose route description is available at the tourist information office. The town, whose urban history dates back to 1333, also tells its story on a guided walk past its churches, held on Thursdays at 1:30 p.m. from May to October.

days_plan.itin_title: Twente in 3 Days: Museums, Gardens, and Medieval Towns

visits.text: Explore Delft's historic center on foot, between the canals and the Markt. The Nieuwe Kerk houses the tomb of William of Orange, founder of the Dutch Republic, and its bell tower offers a view across the whole city. Next door, the Renaissance town hall dates from 1618.

Royal Delft—the Koninklijke Porceleyne Fles—was founded in 1653 and remains the only one of the original 32 Delftware factories still in operation. You'll watch artisans hand-paint blue and white patterns using cobalt oxide, whose blue color only appears after firing at 1,200°C. The visit lasts 1 hour and 30 minutes, and you can observe painters at work in the studio.

The Vermeer Centrum traces the life of the painter born in Delft in 1632. None of his 36 paintings are displayed here, but high-definition reproductions allow you to study his use of light up close. It provides the best context for understanding what you saw at the Mauritshuis the day before.

activities.text: Rent a bike and meander along Delft's canals—the city is flat, and bike paths wind around the bridges and alleyways of the medieval center. In an hour's ride, you'll pass through neighborhoods most visitors never see.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Netherlands Road Trip: Tulips, Windmills, the Delta and Cities of Art

visits.text: The Mauritshuis occupies a 1644 mansion on the edge of the Hofvijver, built for Count Johan Maurits van Nassau. You'll see Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring, Rembrandt's The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp, and Fabritius's The Goldfinch. Allow 1 hour and 30 minutes: the museum is compact but every room is a masterpiece. Beat the crowds by arriving after 3pm or on Thursday evenings.

The Binnenhof is a parliamentary complex whose origins date back to the 13th century under Count Floris IV. The Ridderzaal, the Knights' Hall with its 18 m wooden beams, is part of this historic ensemble. The inner courtyard and the Ridderzaal are currently closed for renovation. To discover the site, walk along the edge of the Hofvijver: you can view the façades of the parliamentary complex from outside and see their reflections in the water.

Madurodam recreates the Netherlands at 1:25 scale: Kinderdijk windmills, Schiphol Airport, Rotterdam harbor, the Royal Palace. It's the perfect place to grasp the country's geography before experiencing it in real life. Allow an hour - it's fun for all ages.

Scheveningen is The Hague's seaside resort, 5 km from the city center. Its pier extends 380 meters over the North Sea, and its fine-sand beach stretches 11 km. Perfect for a late afternoon break before watching the sun descend over the water.

activities.text: A stroll along Scheveningen's seafront at sunset—the Dutch bike here from downtown along the Het Haagse Beek canal. The view of the North Sea, often accompanied by strong winds, immediately sets the tone for the Netherlands.

visits.text: A grayish military port at first glance, but the former Willemsoord naval yard hides one of the country's liveliest museums. The Marinemuseum takes you aboard the submarine Tonijn (78 m, in service until 1991), past the bunks, torpedoes, and periscopes. On clear days, they say you can spot Texel through the eyepieces. Open daily except Mondays outside school holidays.

Sailors simply call it 'De Werf'. The minelayer Abraham Crijnssen is moored outdoors - step onto the deck at no extra charge. The museum traces the history of the Royal Netherlands Navy since the 17th century. Allow an extra 1 h 30 if you visit the entire outdoor site.

activities.text: Board the submarine Tonijn: bunks stacked three levels high, ballast valves, and a 6 m² galley make you understand why crews stayed 6 weeks submerged. The Navy Games let kids test navigation simulators. Combined museum + submarine ticket recommended.

visits.text: The painting is in London, the mill beside the Dinkel: the National Gallery holds a painting of two watermills by Jacob van Ruisdael from around 1650, believed to depict Singraven. According to the local tourist information office, this is the Netherlands’ only water-powered sawmill. Volunteer millers offer tours on Saturday afternoons from April to October for €2.

Mentioned as early as the late 14th century, Huis Singraven houses furniture, paintings, porcelain, and leather bindings. The residence is managed by the Stichting Edwina van Heek, named after the donor already encountered at the Rijksmuseum Twenthe. Guided tours of the house run from Easter to October, and on Saturday afternoons from November to Easter: buy the Huis, Park & Arboretum ticket at the estate shop.

activities.text: Walk the Singraven route described by the tourist information office, a 6 km loop starting at the mill, following the Dinkel along a bike path, and crossing a 475-hectare estate of woods, meadows, and marshes. The full loop takes around 1 hour 30 minutes; alternatively, allow 1 hour for the paths near the manor house.

visits.text: Vast, lively and ringed by Renaissance façades, the Brink is astonishing: for a town this size, such architectural coherence is rare in the Netherlands. Museum De Waag occupies a late Gothic building at the centre of the square; archives mention its weighing function as early as the 14th century, and it became a museum in 1915. The terraces come alive from lunchtime onwards, and a market has been held here on Saturday mornings since the Middle Ages.

Deventer's Bergkwartier is one of the best-preserved historic quarters in the Netherlands, with its medieval alleys around the 12th-century Bergkerk. The Muntentoren housed Deventer's last mint until 1708; the Proosdij is one of the oldest stone houses in the Netherlands. In December, the Dickens Festival transforms this quarter into a Victorian stage set with more than 900 costumed characters.

The Dickens Festival in December: unapologetically kitsch, but the 900 costumed characters walking through the streets of the Bergkwartier end up making an impression. Outside the festival, the Grote of Lebuïnuskerk on the edge of the Grote Kerkhof offers a tower climb to 46 meters above the IJssel.

activities.text: Climb the tower of the Grote of Lebuïnuskerk from Grote Kerkhof square: at 46 metres, it overlooks the bend in the IJssel. Deventer is mentioned as early as the 9th century under the name “Daventre”. The view from the tower confirms its strategic position on the river, which explains its medieval power.

The scent of Deventer Koek has floated over the entire Brink for at least four centuries. This spiced brioche is indeed the town's speciality, sold at the Deventer Koekwinkel on the corner of the square. A bite is a must before leaving. The almond-filled version is the most popular locally.

visits.text: The gardens at Kasteel Warmelo alone make the detour to Diepenheim worthwhile. Across 7 hectares, a French formal garden, an English landscape park, and a pinetum unfold in succession, dotted with 28 sand sculptures whose theme changes each year. The castle, where Princess Armgard lived from 1952, remains private: the gardens open from late April to early October, Tuesday through Sunday, with admission at €9.50.

“Stedeke,” meaning “little town,” is the locals’ nickname for Diepenheim, home to around 2,600 people. Yet the Drawing Centre Diepenheim gives contemporary drawing a national platform through exhibitions, artist residencies, and works displayed in its garden. Arrive after noon: the center opens Wednesday through Sunday, from noon to 5 p.m.

activities.text: From the Warmelo parking lot, follow the Kastelenroute described by the ANWB to Huize Diepenheim, a residence dating from 1648 whose 180-hectare estate remains open to walkers. Return through the village and Rosarium De Broenshof; the full loop extends to Kasteel Nijenhuis and the Den Haller watermill. Wear suitable footwear: around 40% of the route is unpaved.

days_plan.itin_title: Twente in 3 Days: Museums, Gardens, and Medieval Towns

visits.text: Museum Dokkum is housed in the Admiraliteitshuis, a group of buildings, one of which served the Admiralty of Friesland and Groningen in the 17th century, when it was responsible for protecting the coast. The museum covers two thousand years of northeastern Friesland’s history: silverware, textiles, ceramics, and a permanent exhibition on Boniface in a warehouse dating to around 1800. Open Saturday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., closed Sunday; admission €7.50.

If you visit between June 1 and September 15, continue to the Bonifatiuskapel on the Bronlaan, open daily from 2 p.m. to 5 p.m., with free admission. It marks the spot where the Anglo-Saxon missionary Boniface was killed on June 5, 754, and welcomes tens of thousands of pilgrims each year. The small park has fourteen Stations of the Cross arranged around the spring.

“Arm Dokkum,” poor Dokkum: the nickname arose when the Stroobos canal diverted traffic away from the Admiralty town. South of the Markt, the Grote Kerk, or Sint-Martinuskerk, stands on a mound and welcomes pilgrims honoring Boniface. Walk around it before heading onto the ramparts: the loop starts close by.

activities.text: You will follow the Dokkumer Bolwerken, former ramparts with six bastions, along the 2.8 km 11Fountains walk, which takes about 40 minutes. Two windmills still operate here, Zeldenrust (1862) and De Hoop (1849), both open to visitors by appointment. The walk starts at Birthe Leemeijer’s ice fountain, a solar-powered copper sculpture with frost that changes every day.

places.name: Domburg

visits.text: The Marie Tak van Poortvliet Museum showcases the paintings behind Domburg’s artistic reputation. Toorop and Mondrian frequented this resort, but the works on display vary with the exhibition schedule. From September 2026 to June 2027, construction work means the museum welcomes visitors at Noordstraat 13; its return to Ooststraat 10a is planned afterward.

activities.text: Head down to Domburg Strand after the museum to rediscover the simple lines of the shoreline. The rows of wooden posts extending into the sea serve as breakwaters; they also create long perspectives across the sand. Keep your distance from the posts as you walk, and let the wind guide when you turn back, without necessarily planning on a swim.

visits.text: Nicknamed the “Dordtse Dom,” Dordrecht’s Grote Kerk has a tower left unfinished because it was leaning, topped with four clock faces in 1626. Climb its 275 steps, then admire the choir stalls, carved between 1538 and 1542. From April through October, the church opens Tuesday through Saturday from 10:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with the tower open until 4 p.m.; admission to both costs €4.

For us, Dordrecht’s loveliest surprise is the Dordrechts Museum: founded in 1842 with a single painting, it now spans more than six centuries of painting and holds the world’s largest collection of works by Ary Scheffer. Look for Aelbert Cuyp as well, a Golden Age landscape painter born in the city. Open Tuesday through Sunday, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.; €17, free for ages 18 and under.

Huis Van Gijn, on the Nieuwe Haven, shows how a wealthy couple and their servants lived around 1900. Banker and collector Simon van Gijn bequeathed the house to the city when he died in 1922. Climb up to the attic: it houses a collection of 19th-century toys. Open Wednesday through Sunday, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.; €14, free for ages 18 and under.

activities.text: End the day at the Groothoofdspoort, where the Merwede, Oude Maas, and Noord rivers meet. Above the riverside entrance, the Dordtse Maagd, an allegorical figure representing the city, sits enthroned in the “Garden of Holland,” surrounded by the coats of arms of sixteen cities that rose up during the Eighty Years’ War. Return via the Wolwevershaven and Nieuwe Haven, then Wijnstraat and Het Zeepaert, a house dating from around 1495.

days_plan.itin_title: Holland’s Green Heart in 3 Days: Leiden, Gouda, Kinderdijk

visits.text: In August, heather turns purple as far as the eye can see: Dwingelderveld National Park is Western Europe's largest wet heathland, with 3,700 hectares and over 60 pools. Two flocks of Drenthe heath sheep are led by shepherds to maintain the ecosystem. The park is officially the Netherlands' quietest zone.

Officially designated the Netherlands' quietest zone, Dwingelderveld has also become an area where wolves have returned—a presence confirmed in 2024. Visitors must keep a distance of 100 m. Watching migrating cranes from birdwatching blinds in the fall is also popular.

activities.text: Climb the observation tower near Schaapskooi Ruinen: 360° views over the heath and, on clear days, over the surrounding villages' church spires. Walking and horseback routes covering 57 km of marked trails start at the Dwingelderveld visitor center (Benderse 22, Ruinen).

visits.text: A cellar that floats to stay dry: the Edams Museum has this solution in its former merchant’s house. The masonry basin moves with fluctuations in the groundwater level rather than remaining fixed to the ground. The museum also occupies the former town hall; from November 1 to March 31, only the Coopmanshuys opens on weekends, 10 a.m.–4:30 p.m.

Colored light draws your eye in Edam’s Grote Kerk, even before the details of the furnishings. This three-aisled church preserves stained-glass windows and an old library, the librije: here Edam tells a story other than cheese. Admission is free, from April to the end of September from 1:30 p.m., until 4 p.m. in April and 5 p.m. afterward; out of season, access is only possible during events; park near the bus station, ten minutes’ walk away.

activities.text: If you enjoy short detours, Edam’s Voorhaven offers a walk among canals, bridges, and building facades. Continue to the Kaaswaag, a reminder of cheese weighing, then to the Speeltoren. The cheese market takes place on Jan Nieuwenhuizenplein on Wednesdays in July and August, from 10:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Zuiderzee Route: Ports and Villages in 3 Days

visits.text: The Van Abbemuseum is one of the Netherlands' most important modern and contemporary art museums. Its collection includes works by Picasso, Chagall, Mondrian, and El Lissitzky. The 2003 architectural extension creates a dialogue between the original 1936 brick building and a spectacular contemporary volume.

Strijp-S is the former 27-hectare Philips industrial complex, closed to the public for decades - nicknamed the 'Forbidden City.' Now converted into a creative district, it houses lofts in the Anton and Gerard factories, artist studios, galleries, and cafés in the former manufacturing workshops. This is where Dutch Design Week takes place every October.

The Philips Museum traces the history of the industrial empire founded in Eindhoven in 1891 by Gerard Philips—from the first electric light bulb to the razor, by way of radio and television. The interactive presentation is accessible to visitors of all ages.

activities.text: Wander through Strijp-S in the evening—street art covers the old industrial buildings, outdoor seating fills the interior courtyards, and local designer boutiques stay open late. It's the best place to understand how Eindhoven reinvented itself as a design capital after Philips left.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Netherlands Road Trip: Tulips, Windmills, the Delta and Cities of Art

visits.text: A perfect square, and it's real: Elburg's fortified town measures 250 by 415 metres, laid out in 1392 by Duke William I of Guelders to protect his Hanseatic town. The grid plan is flawless—only one street remains curved, the Krommesteeg, because of the terrain. Parking is outside the walls, a two-minute walk away. In summer, crowds can be heavy: arrive before 10 am.

The Vischpoort is the only gate still standing since 1592, when an opening was made in the old defensive tower to let fishing boats pass. On the town side it has windows; on the sea side it has none—its windowless face once served as an oil-lit lighthouse for fishermen. Museum Elburg is housed in the former 15th-century Agnietenklooster, with free entry to the courtyard.

activities.text: The green ramparts are a surprise: the Groene Wallen Wandeling follows the 16th-century fortifications from the outside, between moats and meadows. The complete circuit is less than 2 km. Along the way, spot the Deetman ropewalk, the oldest working rope-making facility in the Netherlands, visible from the Noorderwal.

visits.text: More than 140 buildings brought together: at Enkhuizen’s Zuiderzeemuseum, you move from village to village without leaving the museum. The outdoor area brings together houses and workshops from the former Zuiderzee; the Schathuys displays boats, among other exhibits. Allow a full half day; the museum boat departs from the parking lot at Sluisweg 1.

The Drommedaris resembles a stone prow in front of Enkhuizen’s boats. This fortified gate marked the southern entrance to the town; its rounded form is easier to appreciate from the bridge and quays than from close up. For a break inside the building, head to the Drombar, Paktuinen 1.

activities.text: You’ll follow Enkhuizen’s Oude Haven to slow the pace after your visits. The basin and masts extend the town’s harbor heritage, while nearby streets let you vary the loop without returning to the car. Save this walk for late afternoon, with a jacket even if the sun is still out.

days_plan.itin_title: Zuiderzee Route: Ports and Villages in 3 Days

visits.text: Few regional museums span as many centuries as the Rijksmuseum Twenthe. Conceived by textile industrialist Jan Bernard van Heek, donated to the state by his widow Edwina, and opened in 1930, it takes you from medieval manuscripts through landscapes by Jacob van Ruisdael and Impressionist paintings to Karel Appel and Armando. Allow 2 hours; it is open Tuesday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Adult admission is €16.50, with free entry for visitors under 18.

The clatter of 19th-century looms, when they are switched on, fills the final room of De Museumfabriek, housed in the former Rozendaal textile factory. Along the way, you’ll encounter a mammoth skeleton and a full-size lös hoes, a Twente farmhouse where family and livestock lived under the same roof. Walk there along Museumlaan from the Rijksmuseum Twenthe; it is closed on Mondays.

Designed by Karel de Bazel for textile manufacturer M. I. Menko, Enschede’s synagogue has stood at the edge of the city center with its three copper domes since 1928. Art Deco meets Eastern influences here, and the building is still used for prayer. Visit on a Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, or Sunday from 11 a.m., never on a Saturday; an audio guide is included in the €7.50 adult ticket, and opening hours are shorter from November to mid-February.

The Grote Kerk stands in the middle of the Oude Markt, surrounded by outdoor café seating. Its Romanesque core, dating to around 1200, was expanded around 1480 into a Gothic hall church, and the fire of 1862 left it with large round-arched windows. Look for the 1836 sundial on the wall; to hear the 1892 Van Dam organ or the 49-bell carillon, check the Wilminktheater’s concert calendar.

Romanesque Revival on paper, almost Byzantine beneath its domes: the Sint-Jacobuskerk, consecrated in 1933, crowns the Oude Markt with twin copper domes. Inside, a Pietà by Mari Andriessen and ceramic Stations of the Cross by Charles Eyck complement the melon-shaped vault. If the door is closed, walk around via Walstraat: the facade on that side looks nothing like the one facing the square.

activities.text: If one neighborhood tells the story of Enschede’s resilience, it is Roombeek. On May 13, 2000, an explosion at the S.E. Fireworks depot killed 23 people and destroyed around 400 homes; architect Pi de Bruijn designed the reconstruction, combining housing, workshops, and cultural spaces around the surviving Rozendaal factory. Explore it on foot between the two museums, with the restraint befitting a place of remembrance.

Stop by the Volkspark on your way back from the synagogue: 15 hectares of lawns and ponds laid out in the 1870s by Dirk Wattez, funded by a bequest from H. J. van Heek. Visit Enschede describes it as the oldest people’s park in the Netherlands. Near the large pond, a sandstone lion has watched over the founder’s memory since 1874, and Mari Andriessen’s war memorial hosts the annual commemoration on May 4.

visits.text: In the late 18th century, cloth merchants from Vaals had their fabrics “fulled” at the Volmolen, the watermill in the hamlet of Plaat, just south of Epen. Fulling meant beating wet woolen cloth for a long time to tighten its weave. The mill has ground grain since the late 19th century. After a fire in 1973, it resumed operation in 1977 with a new 5.50 m wheel. Today, its flour goes to bakers in Limburg. Admire the wheel from the path.

activities.text: The murmur of the Geul accompanies much of “Dwars door het Geuldal” (“Through the Geul Valley”), a 6 km loop starting in Epen. The trail crosses wet meadows and flower-filled pastures beneath wooded slopes. On your return, stroll among the village’s half-timbered houses, whose wooden frames are visible on their facades. Allow 2 hours. The loop is not marked: follow it using the Natuurmonumenten app, and wear sturdy shoes, as the paths are often muddy.

days_plan.itin_title: South Limburg in 4 Days: Maastricht, Valkenburg, Thorn

visits.text: Since 1975, diver Hille van Dieren has been recovering what the sea has claimed around Terschelling. His Wrakkenmuseum, on the top floor of an island farmhouse, displays objects from ships dating from 1650 to the present and messages in bottles, and has a room devoted to the helmet divers who searched the wreck of the Lutine, a British frigate carrying gold. Children end up in the pirate garden; opening is seasonal, so check the hours.

Pay your respects to Willem Barentsz as you pass: the navigator was born in Formerum around 1550, and a stone monument on the Hoofdweg commemorates him. Trapped in the ice of Novaya Zemlya in 1596, his crew spent the winter in a cabin made from driftwood and planks from the ship, the “Behouden Huys”; Barentsz died on the return journey in June 1597. Then look for the Spylske Huus farmhouse, built in 1759 south of the village.

activities.text: The smell of coffee and cranberry pastries greets you at the foot of the Koffiemolen, Terschelling’s only windmill. Formerum’s miller bought it in 1876 in the hamlet of Dellewal, near West, to reassemble it here; coffee has been served here since milling stopped in 1964. Order the cranberry pastry or sorbet, two typical island treats.

days_plan.itin_title: Terschelling and Harlingen in 3 Days, Bound for the Wadden

visits.text: The Koninklijk Eise Eisinga Planetarium alone makes the detour to Franeker worthwhile. From 1774 to 1781, wool carder Eise Eisinga installed a solar system on his living room ceiling, driven by a pendulum clock, nine weights, and around 10,000 forged nails, at a scale of one millimeter to one million kilometers. The world’s oldest working planetarium, it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2023: admission requires a reserved ticket.

Museum Martena occupies the Martenastins, a fortified residence inhabited since the 16th century. Its university room brings the University of Franeker, active from 1585 to 1811, to life with portraits of professors, one of the three surviving wood libraries in the Netherlands, and a small orrery. One room is dedicated to Anna Maria van Schurman, a 17th-century scholar who corresponded with Descartes. It opens from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tuesday through Sunday, as well as Mondays from April 1 to October 31.

Twenty-seven colorful coats of arms shine in the stained-glass windows on the second floor of Franeker’s Stadhuis, built from 1591 to 1594 in the Frisian Renaissance style, which partly inspired the Dutch House in Brookline, United States. In the neighboring church garden, Jean-Michel Othoniel’s fountain honors astronomer Jan Hendrik Oort and depicts the birthplace of comets. Twenty minutes is enough for both.

“Hjir rekket de bal it hert,” here the ball touches the heart: the motto of Franeker’s Keatsmuseum sums up the Frisian passion for kaatsen. Opened in 1972, it is the oldest Dutch museum devoted to a single sport, located on the Voorstraat near the Sjûkelân; each year, the PC, a major kaatsen match, returns to Franeker. Check the museum’s website for opening hours before stopping by.

Eleven Cities of Friesland in 5 Days, Along the Elfsteden Route

visits.text: Touristy, sure, but once the tour groups leave after 5pm, Giethoorn's canals fall silent again. The village has no roads in its historic center—only 8 km of canals and 176 wooden bridges. The Dorpsgracht is the main artery, to follow on foot or by boat.

The village was founded in the 13th century by pilgrims who dug peat, unintentionally excavating today's canals. The 18th–19th-century thatched-roof farms are built on artificial islands connected by individual bridges. Visit the Museumboerderij 't Olde Maat Uus for a reconstruction of early 20th-century rural life.

The oars of “fluisterboots” (electric whisper boats) glide silently between the gardens. Moving along the facades at water level reveals details invisible from the towpath. Go early or late in the day to avoid weekend traffic jams on the water.

activities.text: Rent a whisper boat from one of the Dorpsgracht rental shops: no license required, €15–25/hour. Two hours suffice for the complete circuit. Keep your distance from other boats in narrow passages—the canals are sometimes less than 3 m wide.

If you love quiet, arrive before 9am or stay after 6pm: the tour buses are gone and the village feels lived-in again. The northern part (Giethoorn-Noord) is always less crowded than the center, even in midsummer. Paid parking at P1 and P2 at the village entrance.

visits.text: Same name, different church: in Goes, the Grote of Maria Magdalenakerk stands near another Maria Magdalenakerk. Choose the large Protestant church for this stop, with its chapels and organ. From April through October, plan your visit Tuesday through Saturday between 1 p.m. and 4 p.m., except during private events.
Facades are reflected between the boats in Stadshaven Goes. The names Bierkade and Turfkade recall the former beer and peat trades; the harbor tells the city’s story without a monumental sign.

days_plan.itin_title: Zeeland in 4 Days: Harbors, Beaches, and the Dike Route

visits.text: If it rains, take shelter in the Gorcums Museum, housed in the former town hall, built in 1860, on the Grote Markt. It tells the town’s history, including the story of the Martyrs of Gorkum, another name for Gorinchem. In 1572, the Sea Beggars, rebels opposed to Spain, captured nineteen Catholic priests and members of religious orders in the town. They were hanged in Brielle. The museum also displays works by painters from Gorinchem, from the 17th century to the present. It is open Tuesday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. and Sunday from 1 to 5 p.m.; it is closed on Mondays.

Sailboat masts and waterfront terraces: the Lingehaven is the marina in the heart of Gorinchem. Here, the Linge River joins the Merwede, which the tourist office describes as the busiest waterway in the Netherlands. From the quays, watch boats pass through the lock. Nearby, the Tolhuis, built in 1598, was the office where ships paid their tolls. On Saturdays from May through September, climb the 256 steps of the Grote Toren, the town’s great tower, with a reservation through the tourist office.

activities.text: Walk around Gorinchem along its ramparts: a 5 km trail follows the almost intact bastions. In 2021, the ANWB, the major Dutch automobile club, named Gorinchem the country’s most beautiful star-shaped fortified town. Along the way, you pass beneath the Dalempoort, the last of the medieval town’s four city gates. De Hoop windmill is open to visitors on weekends: wooden steps lead to the top.

days_plan.itin_title: Rivierenland in 3 Days: Nijmegen, Loevestein, Gorinchem

visits.text: At 123 meters long, with 72 stained-glass windows, Gouda’s Sint-Janskerk is the longest church in the Netherlands. Its stained glass dates from 1555 to 1603, and according to the tourist office, no other church in the world has preserved as much 16th-century glass; in late August 1939, the windows were dismantled and packed into 201 crates to keep them safe from the war. Visit Monday through Saturday, from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. March through October, and from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. in winter; Sundays are reserved for services.

Museum Gouda occupies a 15th-century hospital, the former Catharina Gasthuis, whose surgeon’s room seems straight out of the Middle Ages. Altarpieces, civic guard portraits by artists including Ferdinand Bol, Gouda art pottery, and Hague School landscapes surround an interactive model of the city in 1562. Open Tuesday through Sunday, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.; a combined ticket with Sint-Janskerk costs €19.90, and admission is free for ages 18 and under.

A simple weigh house, but designed by Pieter Post: the Goudse Waag, designed in 1668, is where cheeses were weighed. The relief on the facade and the scales preserved inside recall that purpose, while a museum with an audio guide tells the story of Gouda’s trade. Open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. April through early November, then from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.; the tourist office occupies the ground floor, a convenient place to pick up a map.

activities.text: Palms slap on the Markt: at Gouda’s cheese market, farmers and traders seal their sales with handjeklap, slapping each other’s hands, and visitors can try it too. Horse-drawn carts bring the cheese wheels to the Waag, where they are weighed on the original scales. Arrive as early as 10 a.m. On other days, head to the Gouda Cheese Experience, Agnietenstraat 21, open daily, with a show inside a giant cheese wheel and a small tasting.

Get your hands in the dough at Kamphuisen, the siroopwafel factory at Markt 69. The syrup waffle is a Gouda specialty: the oldest known recipe, discovered in the city, dates back to the early 19th century. The interactive tour lasts about 45 minutes and includes syrup to taste and a waffle, with prices starting at €11.50. Open Monday through Saturday; the last tour starts at 4 p.m., so don’t leave it until the end of the day.

When the museums close, hop on a bike and head for the Reeuwijkse Plassen, between Gouda and the A12. These thirteen rectangular lakes, formed by peat cutting in the Green Heart, are threaded with narrow roads with water on both sides. The Staatsbosbeheer map suggests routes ranging from 10 to 28 km: 2 hours is enough to ride along the lakes and return to Gouda for dinner. Strong winds make the ride demanding, so save some energy for the final stretch.

days_plan.itin_title: Holland’s Green Heart in 3 Days: Leiden, Gouda, Kinderdijk

visits.text: A large white dome shaped like a parachute dominates the Groesbeek plateau: this is the Vrijheidsmuseum, the Freedom Museum. Its shape recalls the Allied paratroopers dropped around Nijmegen in September 1944. The museum tells the story of World War II from several perspectives: Dutch, German, European, and global. It is open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., with Sunday opening at noon. The Museumkaart, the annual Dutch museum pass, is accepted.

Next, head to Groesbeek Canadian War Cemetery, the Canadian military cemetery, about 1.5 km north of the museum. A total of 2,619 soldiers are buried here, including 2,338 Canadians. On the same site, the Groesbeek Memorial bears the names of more than 1,000 missing soldiers whose graves have not been found. This is a cemetery, not a recreational space: dress modestly and keep your voice low.

days_plan.itin_title: Rivierenland in 3 Days: Nijmegen, Loevestein, Gorinchem

visits.text: Yellow, silver, pale blue: set on its island opposite the train station, the Groninger Museum looks like a set of building blocks floating on the canal. Opened on October 29, 1994, the building was designed by Alessandro Mendini, with Philippe Starck, Michele De Lucchi, and Coop Himmelb(l)au as guest architects; its collections range from Groningen archaeology to contemporary art. Open Tuesday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.; free admission through age 18.

Climb the Martinitoren’s spiral staircase, with no elevator, to the outdoor gallery perched 39 m above the ground. Groningen residents nickname this 97 m bell tower d’Olle Grieze, “the old gray one”; at its foot, the Grote Markt lost its north and east sides in the fire of April 1945, during the city’s liberation. Opens at 11 a.m. (noon on Sundays), with the last climb one hour before the 5 p.m. closing time.

The Martinikerk is well worth its €3 admission fee for its organ alone. Arp Schnitger reworked it in 1691 and 1692, but some facade pipes still date back to the 15th century; beneath the vaults, historic murals and colorful stained glass round out the visit. Opening hours vary by season: check the church’s website before stopping by.

The stadtholders of the House of Nassau wanted a garden sheltered from view: laid out in 1626, the Prinsentuin is still hidden behind its walls, a short walk from the Martinitoren. Enter from the Turfsingel through the Zonnewijzerpoort, whose Latin motto reminds visitors that the past is nothing and the future uncertain. The rose garden, herb garden, and leafy arbor take 30 minutes to explore; open daily from 10 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

“Gasthuizen” or “hofjes” is what Groningen residents call these enclosed courtyards, and the city retains nearly three dozen of them. The Sint Anthonygasthuis, founded in 1517 for the poor, housed plague patients from 1608 to 1644, then people with mental illnesses from 1702 to 1844. Step quietly through its 17th-century sandstone gateway on the Rademarkt side: people live here, so do not force a closed door.

If the sky clears late in the day, save the roof of Forum Groningen for last. This ten-story building by NL Architects opened in 2019, several years late because of the region’s earthquake problems; its terrace rises to 45 m, with the Martinitoren directly in view. Admission is free, the roof remains accessible until 9 p.m., and the Storyworld museum occupies the 7th floor.

There are no more services at the Der Aa-kerk, but concerts, theater, and exhibitions: the Gothic church visible from the Vismarkt has found a new purpose. Its tower collapsed on its own on April 23, 1710, killing two people and crushing Schnitger’s first organ; a new tower was erected as early as 1711. The market fills the square on Tuesdays, Fridays, and Saturdays, while outdoor café seating takes over in the evening.

activities.text: Rondvaartbedrijf Kool departs year-round from the Stationsweg, opposite the train station, for a cruise of about 1 hour around the old city center. Bridges, towers, and medieval merchants’ houses drift past along the canals, with commentary from the skipper. Follow it with a visit to the neighboring Groninger Museum, and look up at the station itself, which the tourist office ranks among the most beautiful in the country.

There is no better place than the Noorderplantsoen to end the day like Groningen residents, gathering around the ponds in fine weather. These ponds were once moats: after the 1874 Fortifications Act, the decommissioned ramparts were incorporated into the park. Allow about 15 minutes to walk from the Grote Markt; in late August, the Noorderzon festival brings eleven days of theater, dance, and music to the park.

Next, follow the Hoge der A and Lage der A, two quays facing each other, lined with 16th- and 17th-century warehouses that once stored grain and peat. Until 1877, the A flowed freely into the Wadden Sea through the Reitdiep: cargo was loaded on the Hoge side at high tide and on the Lage side at low tide. Come at dusk, when the facades are reflected in the water.

visits.text: A bell tower without a church: in Gulpen’s old cemetery, an 11th-century Romanesque tower stands alone. It is all that remains of the village’s medieval church. On Rijksweg, the main road, the Gulpener brewery has been making beer for nearly two centuries. Fifteen minutes is enough to see the tower and cemetery.

activities.text: You’ll climb the Gulperberg, the hill overlooking Gulpen, along some decidedly steep stretches. At the summit, at 156 m, a statue of the Virgin Mary from the 1930s watches over a panorama of hills and villages. On your way down, follow the Gulp, the small tributary of the Geul that gave the village its name. Bring something to eat: several picnic areas have been set up on the slopes.

visits.text: Haarlem's Grote Markt is one of the Netherlands' most beautiful squares, dominated by Sint-Bavokerk - a 1370 Gothic church rising 78 meters high. The 1738 Christian Müller organ was played by a 10-year-old Mozart during his 1766 visit, and also by Handel. Admission is free.

The Frans Hals Museum occupies the Oudemannenhuis, an almshouse for elderly men founded in 1609 - and it was Frans Hals himself who painted the 1664 portraits of the regents of this establishment. The collection brings together more than twelve original paintings by the master along with works by his Haarlem contemporaries like Judith Leyster and Jacob van Ruisdael.

The Teylers Museum is the oldest museum in the Netherlands, continuously open to the public since 1784. Its founder, banker Pieter Teyler van der Hulst, bequeathed his fortune in 1778 to create a place dedicated to science and the arts. You'll see drawings by Michelangelo and Raphael, giant fossils, and 18th-century scientific instruments in their original neoclassical setting.

activities.text: Stroll through Haarlem's pedestrian streets and hofjes - these hidden courtyards surrounded by small houses, founded as early as the 14th century, are a little-known treasure. The Hofje de Bakenesserkamer (1395) is the oldest in the country. Haarlem is connected by train to Amsterdam Schiphol: it is a city of art without the crowds.

visits.text: To clear space for his park, Baron Etienne van Zuylen had the village of Haarzuilens moved about one kilometer. De Haar Castle, the largest castle in the Netherlands, was rebuilt starting in 1892 by Pierre Cuypers, at the Rothschild family’s expense, with running water, central heating, and an elevator. Reserve a time slot; last admission is at 4:15 p.m.

activities.text: Allow at least one hour for the gardens of De Haar Castle, open from 9 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. Together with the castle, they cover 45 hectares, where the Roman garden, maze, and Kruisvijver complement one another. Pick up a walking map at reception, then save the late afternoon for the low-angle light on the facades.

visits.text: Noorderhaven gives Harlingen its postcard setting: a tidal harbor built in 1578, lined with warehouses named Poland, Russia, Java, or Sumatra after trading destinations. On the quay, the town hall, begun in 1730 by municipal architect H. J. Norel, features a sculpture of Saint Michael bearing the city’s coat of arms. Walk around the harbor basin: the city has more than 500 protected buildings.

Step inside the Hannemahuis on Voorstraat: this merchants' house, whose oldest sections date to the mid-16th century, has been a municipal museum since 1957. A genever distillery, Harlingen tiles, silverware, and whaling memorabilia make up the exhibits, and the mirror in the back room has not moved since 1790. Allow 1 hour 15 minutes; the museum is closed on Mondays.

Harlingen’s finest souvenir is still made by hand at Harlinger Aardewerk- en Tegelfabriek. This family business describes itself as the last in the Netherlands to produce tin-glazed earthenware and tiles entirely by hand, a tradition documented in Harlingen since 1598. Stop by on a weekday or Saturday: the workshop and store are closed on Sundays, and guided tours are available only to groups.

If the replica of Willem Barentsz’s ship is docked, head to Nieuwe Willemshaven, a few minutes’ walk from the center. Volunteers devoted about 15 years to this boat, built using period methods and completed in time for Sail Amsterdam in 2025. The lightship Jenni Baynton shares the harbor basin; finish with a beer brewed on-site at Brouwdok.

Despite its name, the Stenen Man is no stone man: it is a two-faced bronze head, a Janus set on a bluestone pedestal, watching over two sections of dike. Erected in honor of Stadtholder Robles after the All Saints’ Flood of 1570, it was rebuilt in 1774. Walk there along Westerzeedijk, near the beach, for sunset.

activities.text: Get off the train at Harlingen Haven, the terminus of the line from Leeuwarden: Rederij Doeksen boats leave right next to the station. The fast boat reaches West-Terschelling in about 50 minutes, while the regular ferry takes 2 hours. Save your visit to Harlingen for the return trip and book your crossing ahead of time, especially in summer.

visits.text: Fairy-tale pages hanging on brick walls: the Anton Pieck Museum set up shop in this small Hanseatic town in 1984 on purpose — its medieval streets look exactly like the scenes the artist drew. The museum, opened by Pieck himself at age 89, reconstructs his original studio in the basement with his 1,500-kg engraving press. Adult entry around €12.50.

Born in 1895 in Den Helder, Anton Pieck designed the Sprookjesbos at Efteling and illustrated dozens of books and calendars recognisable throughout the Netherlands. A drawing teacher for forty years, he stayed true to his romantic style in the face of every modernist movement. The artistic school of the time saw it as mere nostalgia; his prints still sell in their thousands today.

activities.text: If you appreciate old organs, the route between the museum and the De Fortuin windmill passes through the Dijkpoort, one of Hattem's two medieval gates. The 1742 mill is sometimes in operation at weekends. The small town can be explored entirely on foot in under an hour; the views over the IJssel from higher ground are among the most unobstructed in the region.

visits.text: A fabric store from 1935 that still looks modern: that’s the Glaspaleis, Heerlen’s “glass palace.” Merchant Peter Schunck wanted to display his goods in bright light. Architect Frits Peutz therefore suspended a glass envelope on three sides of a concrete structure. Designated a national monument in 1995, the building now houses SCHUNCK, which brings together an art and architecture museum and a public library. Step inside the building, open to the public along with its library, to see the city through the glass.

Kasteel Hoensbroek, about 5 km northwest of central Heerlen, is one of the largest castles in the Netherlands. It takes its name from the knight Herman Hoen, who had its tall round tower built around 1360. Four wings surround a courtyard, all encircled by moats—ditches filled with water. The castle is generally open from 10 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. Reserve a time slot online for free to ensure you can enter at your chosen time.

activities.text: Around the Glaspaleis, you’ll come across several Heerlen Murals, the large paintings that cover building facades, mainly downtown. The city has more than a hundred murals, large and small, and regularly adds more. To plan your route, download the free Street Art Cities app: it locates each work and provides its title, artist, and a short description.

visits.text: A vanished castle, but a layout you can still trace: only the outline of Slot Heusden remains. In 1680, lightning struck the keep, which served as a gunpowder magazine; the explosion devastated the castle, and clearing the rubble took seven weeks. Its outline was reconstructed in 1987–1988. Walk around the site to appreciate its scale.

In Heusden’s Stadshaven, near the Vismarkt, you’ll hear sailboat rigging clinking against the masts. The Vismarkt, a former fish market dating from 1796, has a U-shaped gallery supported by Doric columns of bluestone. Beside it, the customs clerks’ house has been rebuilt. Save this spot for a drink before dinner at the end of the day.

You’ll get a sense of Heusden’s layout from the 30 m² scale model at the Bezoekerscentrum, in the former town hall. A film recounts the reconstruction of the ramparts, begun in 1968 using a 1649 plan by Blaeu and honored with the Urbes Nostrae Award in 1980. The tourist information desk is open daily, generally from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m.

If you arrive on a Friday afternoon, step inside the Gouverneurshuis, a residence built in 1592 and remodeled in 1733 for Governor Van Friesheim. Engravings, old maps, scale models, and drinking glasses from the former water management authority, the waterschap, tell the story of the Heusden and Altena regions. On Fridays, the museum opens from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m.; its garden of fruit trees invites you to take a break.

activities.text: Three windmills stand watch over Heusden’s ramparts, and none is original to the site. The one by the harbor comes from Lommel, Belgium: dating from 1752, it was reassembled here in 1971; the others date from 1973 and 1974. Complete the circuit of the bastions above the Bergsche Maas at sunset; the sails turn on the first Saturday of the month.

days_plan.itin_title: Western Brabant in 3 Days: Breda, Biesbosch and Heusden

visits.text: Museum Hindeloopen offers the best introduction to this city, a member of the Hanseatic League since 1368. Behind the church, beneath a sculpted figure of Justice above the door, several rooms showcase local dress, Hindeloopen’s brightly colored painting on walls and furniture, and the history of its fishermen, merchants, and harbor. In season, it opens Monday through Saturday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., and Sunday from noon.

From modest beginnings in 1983, the Fries Schaatsmuseum now claims the world’s largest collection of ice skates. Its Elfsteden room devotes a display case to each winner of the Elfstedentocht, with medals and trophies, while reconstructed workshops depict a forge, a tannery, or a pottery workshop. Allow 1 hour on Kleine Weide: it opens from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Monday through Saturday, and from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Sunday.

activities.text: You can walk around Hindeloopen in 25 minutes on the 1.8 km 11Fountains walking route. It starts at Shen Yuan’s fountain, a tree of life surrounded by a stag and a doe drawn from the coat of arms, where you can sit on giant antlers. It passes the Grote Kerk, whose tower dates from 1593, the 17th-century locks, and the Sylhús with its wooden bell turret.

visits.text: Fishermen say the tide here rises faster than a man can run. The large sculpture on the dike depicting two women waiting for high tide captures the perpetual waiting that sets the rhythm of this coast. Holwerd gives access to the Netherlands' largest salt marsh area: the Noard-Fryslân Bûtendyks.

The Noard-Fryslân Bûtendyks, the Netherlands' largest salt marsh area, begins just behind the dike. The Kees Weverswadpost birdwatching blind lets you observe avocets, plovers, and ducks without disturbing them. Free access, on foot from the village.

activities.text: Take the Wagenborg ferry from Holwerd: the crossing takes 50 minutes and passes sandbanks where seals bask. The regular ferry departs hourly in high season; the fast ferry makes the crossing in 20 minutes for a surcharge. Book online for bikes.

visits.text: Roode Steen invites you to look above the outdoor tables: its facades form an open-air gallery of architecture. This central square in Hoorn brings together traces of the trading town; look for the coats of arms before heading to nearby Kerkplein. Start with this outdoor section so you don’t have to depend on museum opening hours.

The best angle on the Hoofdtoren is found from the quays, letting the boats into the frame. The tower was part of Hoorn’s former defenses; the figures of the Jongens van Bontekoe add a detail to spot near the water. Stick to the accessible areas around it and watch your step on wet pontoons.

activities.text: You’ll walk from Oostereiland to the Oosterpoort, moving from the harbor to Hoorn’s former boundaries. On the island, the buildings of a former prison have found new uses; the gate then leads to a walk near the park. Complete the loop on foot.

days_plan.itin_title: Zuiderzee Route: Ports and Villages in 3 Days

visits.text: If you pass through Hoorn between 11 a.m. and noon, Monday through Saturday, the Sint-Janskerk welcomes you inside. This 13th-century church is the island’s oldest building; restored from 1963 to 1969, it displays beneath its tower the coins and fragments found during the restoration work. Look up at the “Sjouw,” a ball that was hoisted to announce mealtime to workers in the fields.

activities.text: Follow the Kabouterpad, the gnome trail laid out in the woods at Hoorn, especially if you’re traveling with children. The village was home to Jean Dulieu, the writer and illustrator who created Paulus de boskabouter, the woodland gnome. 30 minutes is enough; save some energy for the Boschplaat, a few kilometers farther east.

days_plan.itin_title: Terschelling and Harlingen in 3 Days, Bound for the Wadden

visits.text: Built in 1711 in the Zaanstreek, the De Rat sawmill was dismantled and transported across the Zuiderzee in 1828 to be installed in IJlst. Logs wait in the Geeuw, the old waterway to Sneek, because wet wood warps less. The mill is open for visits on Saturdays from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. year-round, as well as Wednesday through Friday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. from May through September. Outside opening days, admire its sails from the Sneekerpad.

Wood shavings, workbenches, and rows of hand planes: the Museum en Werkplaats Houtstad IJlst tells the story of this woodworking city in a workshop that still operates. Jan Nooitgedagt began making planes and chisels here in 1865, and his factory also produced ice skates and wooden toys. Visit in the afternoon, from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. according to the tourist office, and leave with a replica tool.

activities.text: Allow 35 minutes for IJlst’s 2.6 km 11Fountains walk, starting at Shinji Ohmaki’s Immortal Flowers fountain, a black pot filled with stinzen flowers that enters into a dialogue with ikebana. The path follows the gardens on both banks of the Ee, the only ones to have survived intact in the Netherlands according to friesland.nl, then passes the Geeuwbrug and the Nooitgedagt factory chimney.

visits.text: Spend a magical day at Efteling, the largest theme park in the Netherlands and the fourth-largest in Europe. This legendary attraction in the province of Brabant has enchanted young and old for decades with its fairytale worlds and thrilling rides.

Immerse yourself in the famous Fairy Tale Forest where the stories of Little Red Riding Hood, Mother Holle, and Sleeping Beauty come to life. These enchanting displays, created with remarkable attention to detail, delight visitors of all ages.

activities.text: Take on the park's six roller coasters, from classic wooden ones to ultra-modern attractions. Thrill-seekers will find plenty to enjoy among the water rides and dark rides that have made Efteling famous.

Explore the different themed kingdoms of the park that combine tradition and innovation. Efteling has preserved its nostalgic charm while offering contemporary attractions, creating a unique experience in Europe.
