visits.text: Kampen's own residents call their town an “open-air museum”. It's not an exaggeration: with nearly 500 monuments in its historic centre alone, Kampen packs more heritage per square metre than many provincial capitals. The square around the golden bridge—adorned with gold wheels since the Middle Ages—and the IJssel quays form a harmonious whole that is still full of life.

Built in the 14th century, the Bovenkerk, or Sint-Nicolaaskerk, dominates the IJssel waterfront with its Gothic nave. It houses an impressive organ and stained glass worth lingering over. A few steps away, the Koornmarktspoort is the town's oldest medieval gate — you can climb it for a panorama over the river. Kampen was also the first Dutch town to produce its own cigars: the De Eenhoorn factory still offers tours.

activities.text: The IJssel waterfront stretches for several hundred metres under the setting sun. Walk the quays up to the town bridge to see the golden wheels that have adorned its pylons since the Middle Ages. The waterside terraces come alive in the evening; the Proeflokaal De Stomme van Campen, with a view over the IJssel, serves local beers.

visits.text: Rolduc Abbey is worth planning your day around its guided tour. Founded in 1104 by the priest Ailbertus on the outskirts of Kerkrade, it preserves a crypt consecrated in 1108, where every column has different decoration. The abbey also operated its own coal mines starting in 1742. The 1-hour-30-minute tour (€9) takes you through the church, the crypt, and the Rococo-style library, with its sweeping curves. Tours start on Wednesdays and Saturdays at 3:30 p.m. and Sundays at 10:30 a.m.

days_plan.itin_title: South Limburg in 4 Days: Maastricht, Valkenburg, Thorn

visits.text: Admire the 19 historic windmills of Kinderdijk, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997. These 18th-century mills, built to pump water from the polders, form one of the most impressive and best-preserved groups of windmills in the Netherlands.

Visit the museum windmill to understand the ingenious workings of these hydraulic machines. These mills pump water into the “Nieuwen Waterschap,” which flows into the Lek River, allowing farmland to be maintained below sea level.

activities.text: Cycle along the paths that wind between the majestic windmills. In any season, these giants with their turning sails offer a fascinating spectacle, especially at sunset when their silhouettes stand out against the fiery sky.

Discover the history of the Dutch people's age-old struggle against water at this iconic site. These windmills bear witness to the ingenuity of a people who reclaimed land from the sea and kept it habitable for centuries.

visits.text: 32 km of dyke inaugurated in 1932: the inland Zuiderzee became the IJsselmeer, and two provinces were connected. Engineer Cornelis Lely drew up the plans in 1891 and died in 1929, three years before his work was completed. At Kornwerderzand, view the dyke and the locks between the IJsselmeer and the Wadden Sea. The Vlietermonument, with its observation tower designed by architect Dudok, is closed to the public during the works: do not plan to climb the tower.

According to Dutch historical sources, a few hundred soldiers held Kornwerderzand against a German cavalry division in May 1940, and the Blitzkrieg stopped here. Kornwerderzand remains the only defensive position where German troops were repelled during the May 1940 invasion. The 17 original casemates can be visited at the Kazemattenmuseum. Entry included in the Atlantikwall pass.

activities.text: Visit the Kazemattenmuseum Kornwerderzand: the bunkers and uniforms date from the period, and the original lock control panel is still in place. The adjacent Afsluitdijk Wadden Center opened in 2018 to put the dike's future in the context of rising water levels. Allow 1.5 hours for both sites.

visits.text: The seals have moved: since spring 2025, the care center founded in Pieterburen more than fifty years ago has been based at the Werelderfgoedcentrum Waddenzee in Lauwersoog. In this building designed by the Danish architecture firm Dorte Mandrup, you can view the seal hospital through glass, attend talks by the caretakers, and explore rooms devoted to the tides. Finish on the rooftop with panoramic views, facing Schiermonnikoog and the Lauwersmeer; open daily from 10 AM to 5 PM, with cheaper tickets online.

activities.text: Board at Lauwersoog harbor, created when the Lauwerszee was closed off in 1969, to see harbor seals and gray seals on the Wadden sandbanks. The Zeehondencentrum trip lasts about 2 hours; Beleef Lauwersoog also offers a 45-minute lifeboat trip for up to twelve passengers, including 15 minutes near the seals. Choose a departure that fits around your walk and bring binoculars.

visits.text: A cool mist envelops two 7-meter-tall children’s faces as you leave the station: this is Love, Jaume Plensa’s fountain on Leeuwarden’s Stationsplein. With their eyes closed, they are dreaming, explains the artist, who was inspired by the morning mist over the Frisian meadows. It opens the 11Fountains series, one per city, created for Leeuwarden-Fryslân’s year as European Capital of Culture in 2018. Step into the cloud, about 2 meters high; from November 1 until spring, the fountain is shut down for the season.

Leeuwarden’s most endearing tower is the one that was never finished. Construction of the Oldehove began in 1529, but it started leaning while work was underway and was abandoned in 1533: it stands barely over 39 meters tall, with its top about 2 meters off vertical. You can climb its 183 steps daily from April through the last weekend in October, from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m., for €3.50; cards and cash are accepted.

Set aside 2 hours for the Fries Museum on Wilhelminaplein to understand the province before exploring it. The “Story of Friesland” exhibition traces Frisian history, the fighter Grutte Pier has a place in the collections, and a section follows Mata Hari, born in Leeuwarden in 1876, who became a worldwide media sensation. Temporary exhibitions round out the displays, including one devoted to the legendary King Redbad in 2026–2027. The museum is open Tuesday through Sunday, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., with tickets available online.

In 1898, M. C. Escher was born in the city palace that now houses the Keramiekmuseum Princessehof, founded in 1917 by collector Nanne Ottema. The national ceramics museum holds about 35,000 objects, including the Netherlands’ largest collection of Chinese porcelain, imperial pieces, and an overview of Dutch Art Nouveau and Art Deco ceramics from 1880 to 1930. Leave time for Karel Appel’s sculpture; the museum is open Tuesday through Sunday, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.

If a concert is scheduled, step inside the Grote of Jacobijnerkerk to hear its Baroque organ, built by Christian Müller between 1724 and 1727, with 37 stops across three manuals. Begun in 1275 for a Dominican friary, it is Leeuwarden’s oldest building; its choir houses the crypt of the Frisian Nassau family, ransacked in 1795 and restored in 1948. Saint-Saëns and Albert Schweitzer played here. Check the church’s calendar before visiting, as opening hours vary with events.

A prison where people come to read and dine: the Blokhuispoort, a fortress commissioned in 1499 by Stadtholder Willibrord de Schaumburg, served as a prison for around 130 years, until 2007. Today it houses the dBieb library, artisan shops in former cells, the Proefverlof restaurant, and a small free museum. Guided tours led by former guards can be booked online.

activities.text: Board Leeuwarden’s canal cruise beneath the orange flag on Willemskade for 1 hour on the canals via the Prinsentuin. On board, the guide projects old photographs, drawings, and paintings onto a large screen, comparing Leeuwarden past and present. The longer cruise, lasting 1 hour 30 minutes, covers all the canals and is known as Leeuwarden’s “8.” Expect to pay €10 for the short cruise and €15 for the long one.

At dusk, stroll to the Waagplein, where the small Waag was used to weigh butter and other goods from 1598 to 1884, near the statue of a Frisian horse. On Over de Kelders, the statue of Mata Hari commemorates the dancer born in Leeuwarden in 1876. End the evening with a glass of beerenburg, the Frisian herb-infused genever.

visits.text: A two-thousand-year-old Egyptian temple stands in the entrance hall of a Dutch museum: the Temple of Taffeh is the centerpiece of the Rijksmuseum van Oudheden. Dismantled in Nubia during the international campaign to save its monuments, it was reassembled stone by stone in Leiden. Around it are more than 150,000 objects from Egypt, the Near East, Greece, Rome, and the ancient Netherlands, including the coffin of the priest Panehsy, covered in hieroglyphs and winged gods. Arrive when the museum opens at 10 a.m. and start with Egypt.

In our view, no museum tells Leiden’s story better than Museum De Lakenhal. The building, dating from 1640, was the cloth merchants’ hall; it became the municipal museum in 1874 and reopened in 2019 after an award-winning renovation. Look for Lucas van Leyden’s Last Judgment, then Rembrandt’s Spectacles Seller, one of the five paintings in his Senses series. The museum is open Tuesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.: allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

The birthplace of the Dutch tulip fits into a square plot measuring about 35 by 40 meters. This garden of Carolus Clusius, reconstructed in 2009, lies within Hortus botanicus Leiden, founded in 1590 and the oldest botanical garden in the Netherlands. After arriving in 1593, the botanist grew the tulips here that laid the foundations for the Dutch bulb industry. Continue to the Japanese garden dedicated to Von Siebold and the orangery dating from the 1740s. Come for the blooms in spring; when it rains, take shelter in the greenhouses.

If you could choose just one viewpoint over Leiden, climb De Burcht. This entirely artificial mound, about ten meters high, supports a circular defensive wall whose wall walk overlooks the rooftops of the center, where the Rhine, Mare, and Vliet meet. Pass through the wrought-iron gate dating from 1653: admission is free, and twenty minutes is enough, ideally between two museums.

A museum windmill that still springs to life: at Molenmuseum De Valk, the original milling mechanism is still used from time to time. This tower mill from 1743, the last of the nineteen windmills that once stood on Leiden’s ramparts, has seven levels and preserves the only surviving urban miller’s home in the Netherlands on its ground floor. It is a nod to Rembrandt, born in Leiden in 1606, the ninth child of a miller. Closed Mondays; the stairs are steep, so keep your hands free.

The Pieterskerk has held no services since 1971, but its floor slabs preserve some famous names: John Robinson, pastor to the Pilgrims, was buried here in 1625, as were the painter Jan Steen and the scholar Herman Boerhaave. Robinson’s congregation had lived in Leiden for nearly twelve years starting in 1609. The church is open Tuesday through Sunday, from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m., with admission costing €6; the small Pilgrim Museum at Kloksteeg 16 is open in the afternoons Wednesday through Sunday.

activities.text: Take a canal cruise lasting about 1 hour with Rondvaart Leiden or one of the other companies in the center. From the water, the historic heart unfolds along 28 kilometers of canals and no fewer than 88 bridges, and you see the facades differently at quay level. Schedule the cruise for late afternoon if that day’s departure times allow, and book your time slot ahead in fine weather.

An unobtrusive gateway, then silence, a lawn, and low houses: Leiden has more than 35 hofjes, courtyards lined with homes that are still occupied. Most are open during the day, but access rules vary from one courtyard to another and are posted at the entrance. The Sint Anna Aalmoeshuis, with its chapel and small museum, can only be visited on Saturdays from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m. Speak softly: residents live here.

days_plan.itin_title: Holland’s Green Heart in 3 Days: Leiden, Gouda, Kinderdijk

visits.text: The best time to see Exposure is in the evening, when its steel silhouette stands out against the Markermeer. Antony Gormley used his own body as the model for this crouching man, 26 m tall and weighing 60 tonnes, unveiled on September 17, 2010, on the Markerstrekdam near the Houtrib locks. In an ironic twist, if the dike is raised to cope with rising water levels, the statue could gradually become buried. Arrive before sunset.

From the Ice Age to the present, the Batavialand museum tells the story of the polders and the Zuiderzee coast, with a film showing the landscape 7,000 years ago. The wrecks in the Lost Ships exhibition are a reminder that Lelystad stands on a former seabed. Open Tuesday through Sunday from 11 a.m., the museum deserves close to two hours; bring a bank card, as cash is not accepted.

activities.text: Next, visit the Batavialand shipyard, where the replica of the Batavia was built between 1985 and 1995 using 17th-century materials and methods. Rope making, nail forging, and wood chiseling are among the workshop activities families can try together. The original ship sank off Australia in 1629. Since October 2, 2026, its replica has been on the museum grounds awaiting restoration: boarding is currently suspended.

days_plan.itin_title: Flevoland in 3 Days: Polders, Marker Wadden, and Urk

visits.text: Visit Keukenhof, nicknamed the Garden of Europe and considered one of the most beautiful spring gardens in the world. With over seven million tulips, daffodils, and hyacinths in bloom, this 32-hectare park offers an absolutely spectacular explosion of colors from March to May.

Discover the fascinating history of the tulip and 17th-century “Tulipmania” through the park's exhibitions. This period when bulbs were worth more than houses reflects the Dutch passion for this flower that has become a national symbol.

activities.text: Admire the 50 sculptures by Dutch artists scattered throughout the park, making Keukenhof the largest sculpture park in the Netherlands. Contemporary art is in harmonious dialogue with the floral arrangements in a successful marriage of nature and culture.

Embark on an excursion by traditional wooden boat through the surrounding tulip fields. These old boats, once used by gardeners, offer a unique perspective on the multicolored rows stretching endlessly into the distance.

days_plan.itin_title: Netherlands Tour: Tulips, Windmills and Villages
Southern Netherlands Road Trip: Tulips, Windmills, the Delta and Cities of Art

places.name: Loonse En Drunense Duinen

visits.text: The Randwal van Giersbergen, a high, tree-covered dune ridge, protected the hamlet from encroaching sand. In the 19th century, trees were planted around it to stabilize the dunes; from the ridge, your gaze sweeps across the pale expanse of sand. Start here, at the Giersbergen entrance in the north of the park.

activities.text: A little Sahara in Brabant? The image fits the Loonse en Drunense Duinen, a national park of around 3,500 hectares combining forests, heathland, and dunes. According to the ANWB, it contains one of Western Europe’s largest areas of drifting sand. The bare sand heats up in the sun, then cools by tens of degrees at night. You can walk freely across the open sandy areas, respecting protected zones and posted instructions.

days_plan.itin_title: Western Brabant in 3 Days: Breda, Biesbosch and Heusden

map_keywords: Nationaal Park Loonse en Drunense Duinen

visits.text: The bright red tower of St. John’s Church (Sint-Janskerk) catches your eye from the Vrijthof, Maastricht’s largest square. Right next door stands the Basilica of St. Servatius (Sint-Servaasbasiliek). According to tradition, Bishop Servatius, who died around 384, is buried here. The current church is believed to be the fourth built over his tomb. Its treasury displays the Noodkist, a large 12th-century reliquary chest. Adult admission costs €7.50, and accompanied visitors ages 17 and under enter free. On Sundays, the basilica does not open until 11:30 a.m.

The Basilica of Our Lady (Onze-Lieve-Vrouwebasiliek) has a massive sandstone facade, almost without windows, built in the early 11th century. Stones probably taken from the old Roman camp were reused in its lower section. Locals, however, mainly come for the Sterre der Zee, “Star of the Sea”: a 15th-century statue of the Virgin Mary housed in a chapel near the entrance. It is carried in procession through the city twice a year. Allow less than ten minutes to walk here from the Vrijthof.

Nearly 800 years old: that is the age of the Helpoort, the oldest surviving city gate in the Netherlands. It was built around 1229 along with Maastricht’s first city wall. It marks the entrance to the Jekerkwartier, the neighborhood crossed by the small Jeker River. The gate now houses the Vestingmuseum, the city’s fortifications museum. It is open Wednesday through Sunday, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. Admission costs €6 for ages 12 and up.

A Gothic church with no Mass, but plenty of readers: Boekhandel Dominicanen is a bookstore that has occupied the 13th-century Dominican church since 2006. Beneath the vaults, old paintings still decorate the ceiling and walls. A monumental steel bookcase holds the books. In 2025, it was voted the world’s most beautiful bookstore from among nineteen contenders. Arrive at opening time to photograph the nave without the crowds.

The Markt is worth a detour even when there is no market, thanks to the city hall (Stadhuis) standing on the square. Architect Pieter Post designed it, and the city council moved in in 1664. Much of the interior still dates from the 17th century. Its history recalls an unusual arrangement: for centuries, Maastricht had two lords at once, the Duke of Brabant and the Prince-Bishop of Liège, who governed the city jointly. Look up at the octagonal bell tower, topped with a carillon.

If you cross just one bridge in Maastricht, choose the Sint-Servaasbrug, often described as the oldest bridge in the Netherlands. It was built between 1280 and 1298, slightly north of an earlier Roman bridge. That bridge collapsed in 1275 under the weight of a procession, killing 400 people. The seven stone arches were largely rebuilt after World War II. Walk across to the east bank, then turn around to see the old town along the Meuse.

The Bonnefanten is easy to spot from afar thanks to its tower topped with a rocket-shaped dome, designed by architect Aldo Rossi. Inside, Old Masters share space with modern and contemporary art: just a few galleries take you from one century to another. The museum is in the Céramique neighborhood, on the east bank of the Meuse. It is open Tuesday through Sunday, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Adult admission costs €22, and visitors ages 18 and under enter free.

activities.text: After visiting the Helpoort, you can continue with a walk through the Stadspark, where the small Jeker River winds through the grounds. The paths follow the remains of the second medieval city wall. In neighboring Aldenhofpark, a bronze statue depicts d’Artagnan with his sword in hand. The real musketeer died on June 25, 1673, struck by a musket ball during Louis XIV’s siege of the city. In 2026, a skeleton discovered beneath a nearby church could be his: DNA testing has been launched. Take this loop walk in the late afternoon.

South Limburg in 4 Days: Maastricht, Valkenburg, Thorn

visits.text: Perhaps the most moving stop on the trip is the Netherlands American Cemetery in Margraten. More than 8,000 American soldiers who died during World War II are buried here. The walls of the Court of Honor bear the names of 1,722 missing soldiers. Since 1945, local families have “adopted” each grave: they place flowers on it and research the soldier’s life. Admission is free, daily from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., except December 25 and January 1.

days_plan.itin_title: South Limburg in 4 Days: Maastricht, Valkenburg, Thorn

visits.text: Woodwork, fabrics, and small interiors: the Marker Museum offers a close look at domestic life. Housed in six historic houses in Marken, it preserves furniture, costumes, and fishing memorabilia; the old smoke venting systems also reveal how the homes were used. Open daily from late March through September, 10 a.m.–5 p.m., and in October, 11 a.m.–4 p.m. (Sunday noon–4 p.m.); closed November–late March.

activities.text: A former island you reach by car: Marken retains this sense of contrast as soon as you arrive in the Havenbuurt harbor district. The causeway changed access to the village, but the wooden houses and narrow streets keep a pedestrian scale. Walk between Havenbuurt and Kerkbuurt without entering private gardens; save the lighthouse for a longer stay.

days_plan.itin_title: Zuiderzee Route: Ports and Villages in 3 Days

places.name: Marker Wadden

visits.text: The wind whistles at the top of De Steltloper, the observation tower overlooking the entire Marker Wadden archipelago. Below, the De Duikeend bird blind reaches down to water level, with windows for looking beneath the surface, while the Lepelaar bird blind lives up to its name: spoonbills often appear here. Bikes are prohibited, so you explore everything on foot. Save the tower for last, before the return boat.

If a shower threatens, take shelter at the Eilandpaviljoen, the visitor welcome point near the Marker Wadden harbor. Its small exhibition traces the island’s creation and the arrival of wildlife: 193 plant species were recorded in 2021, compared with more than 500 today. Its terrace overlooks the Markermeer, and swimming is allowed at the beach behind the harbor basin.

activities.text: Take the Kustroute instead of the shortcut: this roughly 7 km route follows the shoreline of the island open to the public, passing beaches, mudflats, and bird colonies. Marker Wadden did not exist before 2016, when the first island emerged from sand, clay, and silt dredged from the bottom of the Markermeer. The Netherlands’ first recorded nesting of a long-tailed duck was even documented here. Stay on the paths: the mudflats are dangerous.

visits.text: To finish with a defensive silhouette, Kasteel Radboud reveals another side of Medemblik. Commissioned by Floris V, the castle kept watch over this stretch of coastline; the visit offers a look at the detention areas and views from the ramparts. Payment at the ticket office is by card only; leave time for the audio guide.

The smell of bread accompanies your visit to Bakkerijmuseum De Oude Bakkerij in Medemblik. This museum explores the baker’s trade and baking techniques: everyday work takes the place of kings and battles here. Check the demonstration schedule before visiting; what takes place depends on the day you choose.

Here, steam was used to fight water: the Nederlands Stoommachinemuseum in Medemblik occupies a former pumping station. Its equipment helped drain the surrounding area, and some of the machines still run. To see more than stationary machinery, check the operating days; allow for an additional walk from the town center.

If the door is open, Medemblik’s Bonifaciuskerk offers a break after the steam engines. This Gothic church dates back to the 15th century and recalls another side of the town around its Kerkplein. Keep this stop brief; access to the interior depends on opening hours and events, so plan on viewing the exterior by default.

activities.text: Walk to Meelmolen De Herder in Medemblik before finishing the loop along the quays. This working windmill turns grain into flour, providing a tangible extension of your visit to the bakery museum. Step back along the path to photograph the windmill with its sails.

If the wind lets you linger, Medemblik’s Oosterhaven is a natural continuation of the castle visit. Continue to the Pekelharinghaven: these basins now welcome pleasure boats in the heart of town. Stay on the public quays and choose a sheltered terrace to end the route, before your last night here.

days_plan.itin_title: Zuiderzee Route: Ports and Villages in 3 Days

visits.text: The Oosterscheldekering is the largest structure in the Delta Works - 9 km long between the islands of Schouwen-Duiveland and Noord-Beveland, with 62 steel gates that automatically close whenever the sea rises more than 3 meters above Amsterdam's reference level. This storm surge barrier was inaugurated in 1986 by Queen Beatrix. You can drive across it on the N57.

Neeltje Jans is the artificial island built to assemble the barrier's 65 concrete pillars. Now converted into an information center, it presents the Delta Experience - an exhibition about the catastrophic floods of 1953, which killed 1 835 people and forced the evacuation of 70 000, prompting the entire Delta Works project. The site is around 21 km from Middelburg, a 20-minute drive.

Middelburg is the capital of Zeeland and one of the VOC cities - the Dutch East India Company had its regional headquarters here in the 17th century. The 15th-century Gothic town hall borders the Markt. Don't miss the Lange Jan tower of the 12th-century abbey, visible for kilometers around.

Veere is a fortified village on the shores of Veerse Meer, frozen in its medieval setting. Its grand 15th-century houses on the quay belonged to Scottish wool merchants who held a monopoly on the wool trade with the Netherlands. Today it's a vacation destination for recreational boaters.

activities.text: Walk along the beaches and dunes of the Zeeland coast - Domburg or Westkapelle offer wild dune landscapes opening onto the North Sea. Zeeland has one of the country's windiest and most pristine coastlines.

Zeeland in 4 Days: Harbors, Beaches, and the Dike Route

visits.text: Midsland, Terschelling’s second-largest village, has shops clustered around its church, the Meslânzer kerk. Behind the facades of many listed historic buildings are stores and outdoor seating areas, and Midsland aan Zee beach, one of the island’s widest, is just a few kilometers north. During peak season, the areas around the villages fill up quickly: visit early in the morning.

No admiral or general here: in Midsland, the heroine is an old woman. The Stryper Wyfke statue, erected near the village in 1982, recalls how she is said to have fooled the soldiers and saved the island’s civilians in 1666 during the English raid known as “Holmes’s Bonfire,” while West-Terschelling burned. Stop along the way: 15 minutes is enough.

days_plan.itin_title: Terschelling and Harlingen in 3 Days, Bound for the Wadden

visits.text: To understand this coastline, the Waterlandsmuseum de Speeltoren is worth more than a quick photo of its tower. In Monnickendam, its rooms link the history of the inhabitants with that of the water; images of the interior also reveal how the carillon mechanism works. Outside school holidays, come between 11 a.m. and 5 p.m.: Saturday and Sunday in winter, Tuesday through Sunday from April to October.

Set aside a few minutes to walk around Monnickendam’s Grote Kerk before heading to Marken. This Gothic church stands on the edge of town, rather than in the middle of the harbor. Its contrast with the small surrounding streets makes this detour on foot worthwhile; go inside only if the doors are open, as interior visits are seasonal.

activities.text: You’ll walk along De Haven in Monnickendam to watch the boats and facades from the quays. The town borders the Gouwzee, a body of water connected to the Markermeer: the landscape looks maritime, but you are on the shore of a lake. Keep a windbreaker within reach.

days_plan.itin_title: Zuiderzee Route: Ports and Villages in 3 Days

visits.text: Muiderslot looks like the castle you draw as a child: moats, a drawbridge, and corner towers. Floris V had it built around 1285 and was held captive there before being killed in 1296; the poet P.C. Hooft lived there from 1609 to 1647. Pierre Cuypers, the architect of De Haar Castle, restored it in 1895. The ticket office is open until 4:30 p.m.; a free audio guide is available in English.

activities.text: Since 1673, Muiden’s Groote Zeesluis has had three lock chambers side by side, spanning 50 meters in the center of the small fortified town. Recreational boaters pass through from the Vecht to the IJmeer; across the river mouth stands the Westbatterij, a tower fort dating from 1852. In good weather, choose a terrace beside the lock and watch the boats pass by.

days_plan.itin_title: Utrecht and the Gooi in 3 Days: Canals, Forts, and Castles

visits.text: Even in summer, the chill in the Nederlands Vestingmuseum’s casemates takes you by surprise: the earth covering them maintains a steady temperature. Founded in 1955 by volunteers in the Turfpoort bastion, the museum takes you from underground galleries to cannons, with an exhibition on the water defense lines. Allow at least one hour, Tuesday through Sunday starting at 10:30 a.m.; payment by bank card is required.

Naarden’s Grote Kerk hides its treasure about 25 meters overhead: more than thirty biblical scenes painted between 1510 and 1518 on the oak vault. The tower’s 235 steps lead to a view over the Gooi and the Vecht. Visits are available from the May school break through the fall school break, and at Christmas; admission is 5 euros, 10 with the tower.

Even if the name Comenius means nothing to you, his tomb is intriguing: this Czech educator (1592–1670) rests in the heart of a Dutch fortress. The Comenius Museum traces his life and provides access to the mausoleum, a former convent chapel decorated in the mid-1930s by Czech artists. Visit Tuesday through Sunday, from noon to 5 p.m.

activities.text: Walk around Naarden along its ramparts, ideally on the evening you arrive. Laid out in 1675, the fortress with six bastions and a double moat has been on the World Heritage List since 2021; it is the best preserved of the six fortified towns of the water defense lines. Head back down along Turfpoortstraat: the plaque on the Spaanse Huis commemorates the massacre of 1572.

days_plan.itin_title: Utrecht and the Gooi in 3 Days: Canals, Forts, and Castles

visits.text: Flat roofs, screens of trees, and a large green heart: Nagele is unlike any other village in the polder. Housed since 1998 in the former Catholic church designed by Taen and Nix, Museum Nagele tells how 33 members of the De 8 architects’ group, from Rietveld to Aldo van Eyck, designed this village between 1947 and 1957. Open Thursday through Sunday, 1 p.m. to 5 p.m.; the Museumkaart is not accepted.

activities.text: Next, explore Nagele with the booklet and map provided at the museum. Seven housing clusters, totaling about 300 homes, surround a shared green space on three sides, sheltered from the polder winds by broad rows of trees. A few streets away, Huis Polman is furnished as it would have been in the 1950s, just after the village was built.

days_plan.itin_title: Flevoland in 3 Days: Polders, Marker Wadden, and Urk

visits.text: In 1953, the sea overwhelmed the dikes; at Deltapark Neeltje Jans, the Delta Experience puts this disaster at the heart of your journey. Films and exhibitions explain the structures built afterward, with a detour into the Oosterschelde ecosystem. Book your date using the park’s calendar: the surrounding natural areas are separate from this paid attraction.

If you want to see the Oosterscheldekering without visiting all the attractions, head to the shore near the Topshuis. Beneath the open gates, the tide continues to flow: the storm surge barrier protects the estuary without permanently cutting it off from the sea. The structure’s interior is closed to the public; use the marked outdoor access routes to view it.

activities.text: Sand crunches underfoot in the dunes of Neeltje Jans. After construction of the storm surge barrier, the wind shaped a landscape of marram grass and sea buckthorn on this former construction island. Choose a short loop from the marked routes and stay on the paths, especially near areas reserved for birds.

days_plan.itin_title: Zeeland in 4 Days: Harbors, Beaches, and the Dike Route

visits.text: 130 residents, voted the Netherlands' most beautiful village in 2019 by Elsevier Weekblad. Niehove is a terp—an artificial mound built over two millennia ago to protect the village from floods—and its spider-web layout has been intact since the Middle Ages. Former capital of the old Frisian district of Humsterland.

The 13th-century Romanesque-Gothic church stands atop the terp at a height of 3.7 m, once the village's only stone building. Today it houses the Wierdedorp visitor centre, open from April to October. The paths radiating from the church follow exactly the same routes as they did centuries ago.

activities.text: Walk around the terp on the two concentric paths: the red-brick houses face the center, while their barns face the fields. The view from the top across the Groningen plain on clear days is striking. Duration: a 20-minute walk.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Netherlands: Wadden, Friesland & Groningen in 13 days

visits.text: Beneath the tall trees of Valkhofpark, views open up over the Waal. This park occupies the site of the Valkhof, an imperial castle demolished in 1797. Two remnants have survived. The Sint-Nicolaaskapel is a sixteen-sided stone chapel from the 11th century, inspired by the chapel of Charlemagne’s palace in Aachen. The Barbarossa ruin is the apse, the rounded part of the chancel, of a 12th-century chapel. The interior of the Sint-Nicolaaskapel is used for exhibitions and concerts: check the events calendar before planning to go inside.

If you visit just one museum in Nijmegen, choose the Valkhof Museum, on the same hill as Valkhofpark. It traces more than 40,000 years of local history. The ground floor devotes considerable space to the Romans, whose military camp here marked the Empire’s northern frontier. This past explains why Nijmegen celebrated its 2,000th anniversary in 2005. Look out for a Roman cavalry mask among the exhibits. The museum is closed on Mondays; allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

Severely damaged in the bombing of February 22, 1944, the Stevenskerk once again dominates central Nijmegen. This Gothic church was consecrated in 1273. Its spire, lost during the war, was not rebuilt until 1969. Nearby, on the Grote Markt, the main square, stands the Boterwaag, built in 1612. This was the public weigh house, the building where goods were weighed; it now houses a café. The Stevenskerk is generally also open to visitors on weekdays, but its hours vary with events: check its calendar before your visit.

Lange Hezelstraat escaped the bombing of 1944. Nijmegen’s tourist office describes it as the oldest shopping street in the Netherlands. It has retained houses from the Middle Ages and later centuries. Today, the street is home to artisan workshops and specialty stores. Walk up it at a leisurely pace and step inside the workshops: that is the best way to enjoy it.

Then head down to the Waalkade, the quay along the Waal. Outdoor café seating, lawns, and river views line the waterfront. Look for the Besiendershuis, a 16th-century house. Its name comes from the “beziender,” the official who collected tolls here from passing boats. Nearby stands the Waalbrug, a large road bridge opened in 1936. In September 1944, it was the focus of fierce fighting during Operation Market Garden, the Allied offensive intended to open the route to Arnhem. The quay is flat, making the walk suitable for everyone.

Peaceful and green, Kronenburgerpark nevertheless preserves part of Nijmegen’s military fortifications. You can see a section of the old city wall and the Kronenburgertoren, a tower in the ramparts. A large bastion, a projecting section of the ramparts, completes the ensemble. A stone lion carved in 1886 stands guard. The park also has a deer enclosure and a grotto with a waterfall. With children, it makes a good break between visits.

activities.text: Nijmegen’s most moving moment takes place every evening on De Oversteek, the city bridge opened in 2013. It spans the Waal where American paratroopers crossed the river on September 20, 1944. Since 2014, a silent walk led by a veteran, the Sunset March, has crossed the bridge at sunset. Along the way, 48 streetlights turn on one by one: one for each soldier who died during the crossing. Arrive 15 minutes beforehand.

days_plan.itin_title: Rivierenland in 3 Days: Nijmegen, Loevestein, Gorinchem

visits.text: Marvel at the largest tulip fields in the Netherlands in the Noordoostpolder. This region northeast of Amsterdam boasts over 2,000 hectares of cultivable land where tulips create natural tableaux of brilliant colors at every turn.

Visit the Noordoostpolder tulip information center to understand the fascinating history of 'Tulipmania' and the economic importance of this emblematic flower. Interactive exhibitions reveal the secrets of bulb cultivation and trade.

activities.text: Explore the colorful fields on foot, by bike, or by car as you please. Far from the crowds of Keukenhof, this region offers a more intimate and authentic experience amid the flower fields, with views of multicolored rows stretching as far as the eye can see.

days_plan.itin_title: Netherlands Tour: Tulips, Windmills and Villages

visits.text: Records from 1388 are said to mention it: the Marialinde, a linden tree on De Lind, Oisterwijk’s central square, was voted Tree of the Year in the Netherlands in 2023. The contest organizers estimate its age at around 650 years, though that is difficult to establish. It grows behind the former town hall, built in 1899, near the bandstand: take a seat beneath its branches.

activities.text: You’ll follow the Vijf Vennen-wandeling, a 6.2 km loop through the Oisterwijkse Bossen en Vennen, from the Kolkven to the Voorste and Achterste Goorven. The Kolkven, the largest and deepest of these ponds, is thought to have been carved out by eddies in an ancient river. Park at the Natuurmonumenten visitor center, Van Tienhovenlaan 4, and bring binoculars.

days_plan.itin_title: Western Brabant in 3 Days: Breda, Biesbosch and Heusden

visits.text: Cool stone and scarce light: the north side of the Sint-Plechelmusbasiliek retains the small windows and blind niches of the Romanesque church built around 1180. The treasury holds the silver reliquary of Saint Plechelmus, dated 1480. The church opens only from April to October; its 61-meter tower can be climbed on a guided tour at 2 p.m., Monday through Saturday.

More endearing than a large museum, the Palthe Huis shows how three generations of prominent townspeople lived in the 18th century. A farm building converted into a middle-class residence in the 17th century, it became a museum after Gulia Palthe’s death in 1928 and also houses the town’s collection. Visit Wednesday through Sunday, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., on Marktstraat.

activities.text: “Boeskool-stad” is Oldenzaal’s nickname during Carnival, when more than 100,000 people follow the grand parade. During the rest of the year, walk around Marktplein, at the foot of the basilica, to discover the history of a town granted town rights in 1249 and linked to the Hanseatic League through Deventer’s sphere of influence.

days_plan.itin_title: Twente in 3 Days: Museums, Gardens, and Medieval Towns

visits.text: If you only have time for one part of the Oostvaardersplassen, start at the terrace of the Buitencentrum Oostvaardersplassen, at the junction of Kitsweg and Knardijk. Spoonbills and northern shovelers often feed just below. The reserve, created when the polder was drained in 1968, covers about 5,600 hectares, much of it closed to walkers: marked trails start here. The center is closed on Mondays except in July and August.

Forest ranger Hans-Erik Kuypers says that on a fine June day, a reasonably knowledgeable amateur can hear or see around 70 bird species in the Oostvaardersplassen. To take up the challenge, follow Knardijk to the bird blinds at De Kluut, which is accessible to people with limited mobility, and De Grauwe Gans, reached by a path lined with screens. Red deer, Heck cattle, and Konik horses are often seen, and the white-tailed eagle has nested here since 2006.

activities.text: Wear sturdy shoes for the Boswachterspad Roerdomp, a 5.7 km loop marked in orange starting at the Buitencentrum. The trail follows the Keersluisplas to the De Roerdomp observation tower, then a bird blind. The loop and tower close in January and reopen in spring, usually in May. In the Driehoek area, Konik horses are most often seen in summer and fall, frequently accompanied by starlings and cattle egrets. In May and June, listen for bluethroats and reed warblers singing in the reeds.

days_plan.itin_title: Flevoland in 3 Days: Polders, Marker Wadden, and Urk

visits.text: The Openluchtmuseum Ootmarsum brings together sixteen buildings typical of Twente, including farmhouses, barns, a sheep barn, and a forge, to tell the story of rural life a century ago. The Teutonic Order had its commandery here until 1800, and the small mill house is its last surviving vestige. Arrive before 3 p.m.: from February to October, the museum closes at 5 p.m.

“Kunststad van het oosten,” the art town of the East: Ootmarsum’s nickname makes perfect sense at the Museum Ton Schulten. The Twente painter exhibits his vividly colored canvases here, associated with the movement he calls consensism, and one room hosts guest artists. Admission is €7, free for visitors up to age 18; doors open at 11 a.m. Tuesday through Saturday and at noon on Sunday.

As you walk around the Simon en Judaskerk, look to the left of the last window for the black cannonball dated 1597, a reminder of the siege that drove out the Spanish. Built of Bentheim sandstone, the nave dates to around 1230 and features a Westphalian Romanesque-Gothic style rare in the Netherlands. Return at Easter for the poaskearls and vlöggeln rituals in the church forecourt.

activities.text: Start at the Markt, where the Oude Stadhuis, built in 1778, stands beside the pump that, along with three wells, supplied Ootmarsum with water until 1934. The streets still follow the layout of the fortified town, and the Oostwal and Westwal trace the former ramparts. Step into galleries among the half-timbered houses as you make your way to the Cremershuis, built in 1656.

At just seventy-one meters, the Kuiperberg nevertheless offers views over the hedgerow-lined countryside around Ootmarsum. At the summit, an ANWB viewpoint indicator commemorates the festivities of July 1922; the hill also holds the town’s Jewish cemetery, established around 1786. Walk up late in the day, just west of the center, and remain quiet near the graves.

days_plan.itin_title: Twente in 3 Days: Museums, Gardens, and Medieval Towns

visits.text: A museum lost in the forest, yet this is where the Van Goghs are — not Amsterdam. The Kröller-Müller Museum, opened in 1938 in the heart of De Hoge Veluwe National Park, houses the world's second-largest Van Gogh collection, with nearly 90 paintings and more than 180 drawings. Access requires a combined park + museum ticket; buy it online to avoid weekend queues.

Ninety Van Gogh paintings, and the silence between them. The Kröller-Müller sculpture garden covers 25 hectares of forest dotted with works by Rodin, Moore and other 20th-century artists. The walk from the car park takes twenty minutes; there are no constraints, and it's the largest sculpture garden in the Netherlands.

Jachthuis Sint Hubertus is a total work of art: this hunting lodge by architect H.P. Berlage, the former residence of the Kröller-Müllers, is one of the most important Dutch monuments. Access is only by guided tour, which must be booked online. It's located 3 km from the museum in the park, accessible on foot or by bike.

activities.text: Take a free white bicycle at the Otterlo entrance - the park provides 1,800 of them at its three entrances. This is a way to move freely around the 5,500 hectares of heathland, woodland and dunes in De Hoge Veluwe. Deer and wild boar are easy to spot in the morning on the open heathland.

If you love contemporary sculpture, the Kröller-Müller's 25-hectare garden deserves a visit in its own right, separate from the museum: the works reveal themselves around bends in the woodland paths, without signs. The Museonder, an underground museum about the park's wildlife, is well suited to children and takes less than an hour.

days_plan.itin_title: Eastern Netherlands - Hanseatic League, Veluwe and Achterhoek in 10 Days

visits.text: Pieterburen has only about 290 residents, but this is where the Pieterpad begins, a trail stretching more than 500 km to Sint-Pietersberg in Maastricht, mapped out between 1978 and 1983 by two hiking friends. Follow it a few steps to the Sint-Petruskerk and its 1805 bell tower; the former catechism room houses a tearoom, a handy stop before your walk.

activities.text: The mud grips your boot, then releases it with a sucking sound as the dike disappears behind you. With Wadlopen Pieterburen, the guided walk lasts about 2 hours 30 minutes across the seabed of the Wadden Sea, added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2009: crabs, small fish, and sometimes a seal in the distance. Book this first, for ages 6 and up: departures follow low tide, which may fall at 6 AM one day and at 4 PM a week later.

days_plan.itin_title: Groningen in 3 Days: Wadden Mudflat Walks, Seals, and a Fortress

visits.text: Roermond’s Munsterkerk, a 13th-century church, is the only surviving part of a former abbey. Its four-towered silhouette owes much to architect Pierre Cuypers, a native of the city, who restored it from 1863 to 1890 and added two towers to its facade. In 1992, an earthquake toppled the two eastern towers, which were rebuilt shortly afterward. A statue on Munsterplein honors Cuypers. Start there: the cathedral and the Cuypershuis are just a few minutes away on foot.

When you look up at St. Christopher’s Cathedral (Sint-Christoffelkathedraal), look for the gilded statue of the saint atop the tower. This tower was rebuilt: on February 28, 1945, the German occupying forces blew it up to prevent Allied troops from using it as an observation post. The city was liberated the following day. Reconstruction was completed in 1957, and residents were able to add their names to a parchment placed inside the statue. The Gothic church itself dates to 1410.

At the Cuypershuis, you can see where Pierre Cuypers, born in Roermond in 1827, lived and worked with his family. From this house and its workshops, built in 1853, he oversaw projects such as Amsterdam’s Rijksmuseum, which opened in 1885, and Amsterdam Central Station, inaugurated in 1889. The interactive permanent exhibition shows how he secured and managed these major commissions. The museum is open from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., except on Mondays.

activities.text: Water as far as the eye can see, just west of Roermond: the Maasplassen encompass more than 3,000 hectares of lakes. They were created by gravel extraction in the Meuse Valley. Today, they form the largest network of connected bodies of water in the Netherlands dedicated to water sports. Galloway cattle graze along the flower-filled shores. Rent a boat or a paddleboard for an hour, or settle onto one of the beaches.

days_plan.itin_title: South Limburg in 4 Days: Maastricht, Valkenburg, Thorn

visits.text: Kinderdijk's 19 windmills were built between 1738 and 1740 to drain the Alblasserwaard polders - a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997. You can enter two museum windmills and take the sightseeing boat included in the ticket. Arrive before 10 a.m. to avoid groups, or take the Waterbus from Rotterdam for an approach along the river. Plan a round trip from Rotterdam for this visit.

Piet Blom's Cube Houses (Kubuswoningen) were built in 1984 in Rotterdam: 38 cubes tilted 45° above the Blaak bridge vaults. You can visit one of them, the Kijk-Kubus, to understand how people live inside an impossible angle.

The Markthal is an arch 40 meters high and 120 meters long, inaugurated in 2014 and designed by the architecture firm MVRDV. Its interior vault is entirely covered with an 11,000 m² digital mural depicting a cornucopia—fruits, vegetables, giant insects. Stop here for lunch: around a hundred stalls occupy the ground floor.

Delfshaven is a historic district of Rotterdam that survived the bombing of May 1940. It was from here that the Pilgrim Fathers departed on July 22, 1620, aboard the Speedwell before joining the Mayflower in England. The 15th-century Pilgrim Fathers Church still stands facing the canals.

activities.text: Bike ride through Rotterdam along the Erasmus Bridge and waterfront - the city was rebuilt from scratch after the German bombings of May 1940, and you'll discover architecture unique in Europe, blending brutalism, high-tech, and urban experimentation.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Netherlands Road Trip: Tulips, Windmills, the Delta and Cities of Art

visits.text: Carel Willink's surrealist canvases—camels in front of Versailles, landscapes with a nuclear power station—hanging in the 14th-century halls of Kasteel Ruurlo create a striking contrast. Museum MORE has displayed around thirty of his works in this monumental setting since 2017. Access to the castle rooms requires a museum ticket; the English landscape park and orangery are free.

Kasteel Ruurlo has housed Carel Willink's works since 2017. The initiative came from collector Hans Melchers, who wanted to offer this 20th-century realist painter a worthy showcase. The castle rooms date back to the 14th century and have been restored to combine several centuries of architecture. Together, they form one of Gelderland's most distinctive art museums.

activities.text: Locals call this maze their “dwaaltuin”—wandering garden. The Doolhof Ruurlo, right next to the castle, was laid out in 1891 on the orders of a Miss Van Heeckeren: 1,188 metres of paths within a hectare of trimmed hedges. Open from April to the end of October. It has a different owner from the museum; expect a separate entrance fee.

days_plan.itin_title: Eastern Netherlands - Hanseatic League, Veluwe and Achterhoek in 10 Days

visits.text: Kasteel Huis Bergh dates back to the 13th century — archives mention the site as early as 1227 — and ranks among the largest medieval castles in the Netherlands. Surrounded by moats, it houses a collection of early Italian period paintings, medieval manuscripts and northern European works from the 16th century. The gardens and inner courtyard are freely accessible; the guided castle tour costs €8 per adult.

The chained manuscripts in Huis Bergh's armoury and the black torches of the keep are reminders that this tower has never been captured since it was built. The castle archive, whose oldest document dates from 1227, is one of the best preserved in Gelderland. An audio guide in several languages traces the history of the lords of Van den Bergh.

activities.text: Climb Huis Bergh's defensive tower to see the lands of Montferland spread out towards Germany, just a few kilometres away. The estate comprises around 500 hectares of forests and farmland surrounding the castle. Concerts and exhibitions are held regularly in season—check the programme before coming.

days_plan.itin_title: Eastern Netherlands - Hanseatic League, Veluwe and Achterhoek in 10 Days

visits.text: Sint-Janskathedraal is the pinnacle of Brabantine Gothic architecture in the Netherlands. Built between 1380 and 1530, it rises 73 meters high and stretches 115 meters long. Look closely at its 96 sculpted figures on the flying buttresses - dragons, angels, and fantastical creatures unique in the country. Admission is free; guided tower tours offer panoramic views.

The Jheronimus Bosch Art Center occupies a former church and presents high-definition reproductions of the complete works of Jheronimus Bosch, born here around 1450. You won't travel to Madrid to see the original Garden of Earthly Delights, but here you'll study it centimeter by centimeter through enlargements.

The Binnendieze is a network of partly underground canals that once extended 22 km beneath the streets of 's-Hertogenbosch. Board an electric boat and glide under houses, town halls, and historic cellars - a unique way to see a medieval city from below. The guided tour lasts about 50 minutes.

activities.text: Grab a bossche bol from one of the downtown bakers—this giant pastry filled with whipped cream and coated in dark chocolate has been the quintessential specialty of 's-Hertogenbosch for centuries. Don't miss the buzz of the market square in late afternoon either.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Netherlands Road Trip: Tulips, Windmills, the Delta and Cities of Art

visits.text: Explore Schiermonnikoog, one of the inhabited West Frisian Islands. Declared a national park in 1989, this island offers unspoiled nature with its wild dunes, pine forests and exceptional tidal mudflats listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Discover the Wadden Sea, a unique ecosystem classified as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. This intertidal zone harbors remarkable biodiversity and constitutes one of the last great natural wetlands in Europe.

activities.text: Join a guided mudflat walk with expert local guides. At low tide, you'll explore this fascinating world populated by crabs, shellfish, and migratory birds—an unforgettable sensory experience.

Enjoy Europe's widest beach with its kilometer of fine sand stretching as far as the eye can see. This immense space where sky and sea blend together offers a sense of absolute freedom, far from any urbanization.

days_plan.itin_title: Netherlands Tour: Tulips, Windmills and Villages

visits.text: Nothing prepares you for the outline of Schokland: a former island 4.5 km long, stranded amid the fields of the Noordoostpolder. The first Dutch site inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List, in 1995, Museum Schokland displays footprints more than 4,000 years old, among the oldest in Europe, along with the church dating from 1834. Open from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., except Tuesdays.

activities.text: If you have an extra hour, walk part of the Ruïneroute, a 7.6 km loop starting at Museum Schokland. It crosses the Schokkerbos, passing the ruins of the Ens church and the Zuidert mound, inhabited from the 14th through the 19th century. Here you can appreciate the Schoklanders’ tenacity in the face of the sea, until the evacuation of 1859: around 635 residents were resettled on the mainland, notably in Kampen.

days_plan.itin_title: Flevoland in 3 Days: Polders, Marker Wadden, and Urk

visits.text: In 1673, Louis XIV’s troops occupied Mount Saint Peter during the siege of Maastricht. The city responded by building Fort Sint Pieter in 1701 and 1702 on the hill’s northern slope. The guide shows you the well, the loopholes—narrow openings for firing through—and the dark cannon gallery. Tsar Peter the Great visited this five-sided fort in 1717. Tickets are sold at the Maastricht Underground shop right next door.

activities.text: The cold hits you as soon as you enter the Grotten Noord, the northern caves of Mount Saint Peter: the temperature is 9 to 10 °C. These are former quarries where limestone was extracted for construction, rather than natural caves. This labyrinth once contained more than 20,000 passages. The guide points out names and drawings left on the walls by the people who worked here. The tour lasts about 1 hour 10 minutes: bring a sweater, even in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: South Limburg in 4 Days: Maastricht, Valkenburg, Thorn

visits.text: The region’s most astonishing story unfolded at Slot Loevestein. This 14th-century brick castle was first used to collect tolls from boats. It later became a state prison. In 1619, Hugo de Groot, a jurist whose writings laid the foundations of international law, was imprisoned here for life. In 1621, with his wife’s help, he escaped hidden in the chest used to bring him books. The castle is open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.

The fortress of Loevestein surrounds the castle with earth ramparts, stone bastions, and moats. These defenses, along with the arsenal and barracks, date from the expansion begun around 1575 under William of Orange. Walk around the ramparts: the site stands where the Meuse meets the Waal, in the Munnikenland nature reserve. An adult ticket costs €18, and the Museumkaart is accepted. The castle’s steep stairs make it inaccessible to wheelchair users.

days_plan.itin_title: Rivierenland in 3 Days: Nijmegen, Loevestein, Gorinchem

visits.text: If it rains in Sloten, head to Museum Sloten, in the former town hall built in 1759–1761 on Heerenwal. Its attic houses a collection of magic lanterns, those projection lanterns of old, which the tourist office calls the finest in the Netherlands. The galleries tell the story of the fortified town, complete with virtual reality headsets. From April through the end of October, it opens Tuesday through Friday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., and on weekend afternoons.

The Lemsterpoort, one of Sloten’s two surviving water gates, has a pillory at its foot: the small town once administered its own justice. Right next door, De Kaai grain mill, built on a bastion in 1755, still grinds wheat. It opens on Saturday afternoons from May through September for tours and flour sales.

activities.text: The best of Sloten fits into 1.4 km: the 11Fountains walking route circles the smallest city in Friesland, whose onion-shaped defenses, designed by Menno van Coehoorn, have retained almost all their ramparts and moats. It starts at Lucy and Jorge Orta’s Peewit fountain, a girl holding a lapwing while sitting on a man’s shoulders, above a pile of buckets and canisters.

days_plan.itin_title: Eleven Cities of Friesland in 5 Days, Along the Elfsteden Route

visits.text: Sneek is nicknamed “the city of the Waterpoort,” and its water gate, dating from 1613, earns the title with its two octagonal towers. A fun detail: the clock runs five minutes fast, once giving people time to pass through before the gate was locked for the night. On nearby Hoogend, Stephan Balkenhol’s Fortuna fountain depicts a man balancing on a golden ball. Return after dark, when the Waterpoort is illuminated.

The Fries Scheepvaart Museum on Kleinzand explains why Sneek calls itself a city of water: freight and passengers on the canals, skûtsje sailing barge regattas, Sneekweek, and a room devoted to ice skating and the Elfstedentocht. A fine silver collection rounds out the visit. Open daily from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.; keep your canal cruise ticket for a discount on admission.

Founded in the 11th century according to Sneek’s tourist office, the Martinikerk was enlarged around 1300 and given a three-towered westwork. Tradition holds that the remains of Grutte Pier, the Frisian fighter who died in 1520, lie within its walls, and its Schnitger organ dates from 1710. The church regularly opens to visitors in summer; during the rest of the year, plan to attend a service or concert.

The most entertaining game at Sneek’s Stadhuis is spotting the symbols hidden in its 1763 Rococo facade, beneath the Baroque entrance steps by sculptor Gerben Jelles Nauta. Built around 1478 on the foundations of two fortified houses, the building has been remodeled many times. Then continue to the statue commemorating the origins of C&A, founded in Sneek in 1841 by Clemens and August Brenninkmeijer.

activities.text: You will duck more than once on Sneek’s historical canal cruise: the bridges are low, which is precisely what allows the small open boat to go where larger vessels cannot. In just under 1 hour, the boat operator tells the city’s story and passes through the Waterpoort. Board at the dock opposite the Fries Scheepvaart Museum ten minutes before departure.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Netherlands: Wadden, Friesland & Groningen in 13 days
Eleven Cities of Friesland in 5 Days, Along the Elfsteden Route

visits.text: In Stavoren, the oldest city in Friesland, people still tell the story of the wealthy widow who had wheat thrown into the harbor: the grain is said to have grown on the sandbar that ruined the town’s trade. Her 1969 statue, the Vrouwtje van Stavoren, gazes out to sea from the old harbor. Then walk along the sea lock dating from 1576, followed by the Johan Friso locks, the second of which was inaugurated by the king in 2014.

Water trickles from the lips of a giant fish 8 meters long: Mark Dion’s De Vis fountain, on Stationsweg near the harbor, was inspired by an engraving by Bruegel the Elder in which big fish eat little ones. It expresses Stavoren’s dependence on the sea, with wealth and danger intertwined. Children play in the spray, except from November until spring, when it is turned off.

You’ll understand the fortunes of this Hanseatic city at Museum ’t Ponthús on Hellingspad: a Viking raid, trade with Hamburg, the Blokhuis fortress, fishing, whaling, the railroad, and the ferry. One room, with a film, explores the legend of the Vrouwtje. Hours vary by season: check with the tourist office before visiting.

days_plan.itin_title: Eleven Cities of Friesland in 5 Days, Along the Elfsteden Route

visits.text: The salty wind greets you as soon as you reach the ferry gangway. Texel is the largest Dutch Wadden island, and Ecomare is its heart: a seal sanctuary, nature museum, and starting point for hikes into Texel Dunes National Park. Injured seals are cared for here before being released into the North Sea. Arrive for feeding times around 11am or 3pm.

Ecomare is more than an aquarium: seals, porpoises, and injured birds share open pools. Entry includes direct access to the national park dunes. Adult admission around €13, children €9. Closed Mondays off-season.

A third of Texel's surface is nature reserve, and De Slufter is its centerpiece. This polder, abandoned in the 19th century, was gradually reclaimed by the sea, creating one of Northern Europe's rarest brackish ecosystems. Visitors on foot only; dogs on leash.

Texel's lighthouse, built in 1864 in De Cocksdorp, stands 35 m tall at the island's northern tip. Plan a return trip from the town where you are staying on Texel to reach the lighthouse. Built of red brick, it overlooks the dunes and the Wadden Sea. Climb its 153 steps for views of the sandbanks and neighbouring islands. Open in season; check opening times on Ecomare's website.

activities.text: Cycle to De Slufter, the only marsh with tidal channels on the Dutch side of the North Sea. The rental shop near the Markt in Den Burg offers e-bikes. The complete island loop by bike is 54 km—allow a full day with breaks.

If you love birds, the De Muy sector shelters a spoonbill colony closely watched by local naturalists. A 2-hour guided walk from Ecomare (around €7.50) takes you into the heart of the dunes with an English- or Dutch-speaking ranger.

Rent a kayak at Oudeschild to paddle along Texel's east coast from the fishing harbor. The harbor is the island's only active fishing port; auctions happen weekday mornings. Return for lunch on-site: fresh gray shrimp cost less here than elsewhere on the island.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Netherlands Road Trip: Amsterdam, Friesland, Wadden Islands & Giethoorn
Northern Netherlands: Wadden, Friesland & Groningen in 13 days

visits.text: Whitewashed Gothic vaults and Baroque altars: the Abdijkerk, Thorn’s abbey church, blends two eras. For about 800 years, noblewomen living in a community here ruled a tiny principality with its own currency and justice system, until the French arrived in 1794. The high altar from 1769 imitates marble using stucco, a smoothed and polished plaster finish. In the west crypt, a scale model shows the abbey in the 18th century. From April through the end of October, the church opens Tuesday through Sunday, from 10:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. In winter, it also welcomes visitors Friday through Sunday, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., with exceptions during the holidays.

activities.text: The arrival of the French in 1794 gave Thorn its color. They introduced a tax based on window size. Many residents, too poor to pay, bricked up some of their windows. To hide these scars in the brickwork, they then whitewashed their facades, giving rise to the nickname “white village.” Stroll through the cobblestone lanes of the now-protected center and look for the bricked-up windows beneath the whitewash.

days_plan.itin_title: South Limburg in 4 Days: Maastricht, Valkenburg, Thorn

visits.text: Blown up by the German army on November 15, 1944, Tiel’s Waterpoort (water gate) was rebuilt in 1979. This gate, dating from 1647, closes off the Plein, a square laid out on a former harbor that was filled in. Its role was less about defense than controlling access. It also protected the town from flooding. During floods, residents of the Betuwe, the surrounding countryside, would take refuge in the town. Today, it houses part of the Flipje & Streekmuseum: start your visit to Tiel here.

The Flipje & Streekmuseum, Tiel’s regional museum, is more amusing than most. Flipje is a little raspberry-shaped character who became the mascot of the De Betuwe jam company in 1935. The Tiel factory stopped production in 1993, but Flipje has remained the town’s symbol. The other floors feature archaeology, painting, and local history. The museum opens in the afternoon from Tuesday through Sunday: from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. in April–October (until 4:30 p.m. on weekends), and from 1:30 p.m. in November–March. It is closed on Mondays.

days_plan.itin_title: Rivierenland in 3 Days: Nijmegen, Loevestein, Gorinchem

visits.text: If you want to see the machines running, arrive at the TextielMuseum before 2 p.m. on weekdays or 2:30 p.m. on weekends. Housed in a former textile factory and opened in 1958, the museum includes the TextielLab, where designers and artists weave, knit, embroider, or laser-cut before your eyes. Buy your ticket online; closed on Mondays.

De Pont occupies Thomas de Beer’s former wool-spinning mill, which closed in the face of foreign competition. Opened in 1992, this contemporary art museum brings together more than 800 works by around 75 artists; outside the entrance, Anish Kapoor’s Sky Mirror reflects the sky. Closed on Mondays; open until 8 p.m. on Thursdays.

Books in a locomotive workshop: the LocHal embraces its railroad past. Built in 1932 for the Dutch railways, the hall, around 18 meters high, was used to repair locomotives until 2010 before being named World Building of the Year 2019 at the World Architecture Festival. It stands beside Tilburg station: save it for the end of your stay.

At 13, Vincent van Gogh took drawing lessons in a palace: Tilburg’s Paleis-Raadhuis. King William II had it built starting in 1847 and died a few days after its completion in 1849; the painter Constant Huijsmans taught the young student there after his arrival in 1866. Now incorporated into the town hall, it can be admired from the outside.

activities.text: You’ll end the day along the quays of the Piushaven, a harbor excavated around a century ago for inland shipping, now lined with outdoor seating. Look for the harbor master’s cottage, occupied until 1979, and the manually operated Prinsenhoeven swing bridge. Café Burgemeester Jansen occupies the harbor’s oldest building: perfect for a final drink.

days_plan.itin_title: Western Brabant in 3 Days: Breda, Biesbosch and Heusden

visits.text: In Uithuizen, the Menkemaborg is one of sixteen surviving borgen manor houses, out of more than a hundred homes of prominent families that once stood in the province. A fortified brick house in the 14th century, it acquired its Baroque appearance around 1700, which the Alberda family preserved until 1902. Arrive when it opens at 10 AM: outside July and August, the museum is closed on Mondays, and its season begins on March 1.

If you visit in July, the rose tunnel in the Menkemaborg garden is in full bloom. The formal garden was recreated from a plan dating to around 1705, with 18th-century plants, a sundial garden, and a large maze with an old plane tree at its center. Allow 45 minutes for the orchard of heritage varieties and the vegetable garden; in spring, stinzen flowers line the moats.

days_plan.itin_title: Groningen in 3 Days: Wadden Mudflat Walks, Seals, and a Fortress

visits.text: In Urk, she is simply called “Urker vrouw”: a woman facing the sea from which her husband or son should have returned. Unveiled in 1968 by Queen Juliana, the Vissersmonument lists the names of 368 men lost at sea on 34 marble plaques. Rarely has a number carried so much weight in such a small port. Stop by late in the day when arriving from Lelystad, before dinner in the village.

A lighthouse that causes a ship to run aground: this is the most colorful episode in the history of Urk’s Vuurtoren. During World War II, a keeper switched off the emergency lights, and a boat carrying loot, including 226 church bells destined for Germany, ran aground on the De Vormt shoal; the bells were returned after the war. The current tower has shone since 1845, with a Fresnel lens dating from 1876. You can climb it during Dutch school vacations, except on Sundays.

Built in 1904–1905, Urk’s former town hall houses Museum Het Oude Raadhuis and more than a thousand years of local history: traditional clothing, fishing, trade, and art. You can visit a fisherman’s house preserved in its original state, a reminder of the days when Urk was an island. A virtual reality headset takes you down to a Zuiderzee wreck, probably the schokker UK117. Open Monday through Saturday from 11 a.m., never on Sundays.

activities.text: Then stroll through old Urk, an island until 1939, with its unplanned lanes, small squares, and signs on building facades. The Kerkje aan de Zee, the “little church by the sea” completed in 1786, recalls the island days. Look about 30 m offshore for the Ommelebommelestien: according to the legend told to children, this rock is where babies come from.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Netherlands Road Trip: Amsterdam, Friesland, Wadden Islands & Giethoorn
Flevoland in 3 Days: Polders, Marker Wadden, and Urk

visits.text: Beneath Domplein, it is dark by design: you explore DOMunder with a smart flashlight in hand. In 75 minutes, a guide takes you from the foundations of the Roman fort of Traiectum to medieval remains, ending with the story of the 1674 storm that brought down the cathedral’s nave. Reserve your tour at the information point at Domplein 9: payment is by card only, access is via stairs, and the tour is recommended for ages 8 and up.

The hearts and entrails of two emperors, Conrad II and Henry V, rest beneath the choir of the Domkerk. The choir and transept survive from the Gothic cathedral begun in 1254 and are free to visit; outside, stones in Domplein’s paving outline the nave that collapsed in 1674. Finish at the Pandhof, the cloister garden, open from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., whose fountain depicts canon Hugo Wstinc writing. On Saturdays, the church closes at 3:15 p.m.

Climb the 465 steps of the Domtoren, the tallest church tower in the Netherlands at 112 meters, whose exterior restoration was completed in 2024. The climb is only available with a guide and takes about 1 hour, with stops at St. Michael’s Chapel, the Egmond Chapel, and the bell chamber, where the Salvator bell weighs nearly eight tonnes. Leave your bag in a free locker: bags are not allowed in the tower. On clear days, you can make out Amsterdam in the distance.

A scholarly museum, but rarely a quiet one: at Museum Speelklok, carillons, automaton clocks, and street organs play before your eyes. The guides, often conservatory students, operate the instruments themselves inside the Buurkerk, a roughly thousand-year-old church where the recluse Suster Bertken lived for 57 years, walled into a cell measuring less than four meters by four meters. Choose the guided tour over simply wandering through; a combined ticket with the Domtoren is sold on-site, and the museum is closed on Mondays.

If you visit just one Old Master art museum in Utrecht, choose Museum Catharijneconvent. Housed in a medieval convent, it tells the story of Christianity in the Netherlands through paintings by Rembrandt, Saenredam, and Jan van Scorel, manuscripts, and relics, bringing together Catholic and Protestant art. The English audio guide for the permanent collection is free; admission costs 16 euros, or 15 online, payable by card only.

Utrecht is at its most beautiful when seen from below, at water level. Stretching for 4.1 kilometers, the Oudegracht’s wharves, known as werven, serve 732 vaulted cellars dug beneath the street; as early as the second half of the 12th century, tunnels linked the wharves to the cellars of the houses. Head down one of the stairways and walk along the wharf; since 1996, beer boats have continued supplying cafés by water, just as in the Middle Ages.

The hall at Post Utrecht, on the Neude, was nicknamed the “temple of Posts and Telegraphs.” Completed in 1924 by Joseph Crouwel in the Amsterdam School style, the former main post office now houses the library; beneath the parabolic arches, Hendrik van den Eijnde’s black statues represent the continents. Free admission starting at 9 a.m., 10 a.m. on Sundays.

Small yet revolutionary, the Rietveld Schröder House was built in 1924 by Gerrit Rietveld for Truus Schröder, who lived there until 1985; UNESCO listed it in 2000. Upstairs, sliding and pivoting panels transform the open space into bedrooms. Reserve a time slot, required even with a museum card, and allow 30 to 40 minutes for your visit.

Here, she is called nijntje rather than Miffy, from konijntje, “little rabbit”: the Centraal Museum recreates the studio where Dick Bruna drew for thirty years. Founded in 1838 in a former monastery, the museum claims the world’s largest collection of Rietveld objects and a thousand-year-old boat discovered in 1930. Open from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., except Mondays.

activities.text: Board a boat for 1 hour on the Oudegracht with Rederij Schuttevaer: from the water, the two levels of wharves and building facades make perfect sense. The route glides beneath old bridges, passes the wharf cellars, and frames views of the Domtoren; a digital guide provides commentary in several languages. Prices start at 18.50 euros; save this trip for late afternoon, after visiting the museums.

If night falls early, all the better: the Utrecht Lumen route lights up every evening from sunset to midnight. Stretching 3 kilometers from Domplein, it connects Pausdam, Pieterskerk, Janskerkhof, the Ganzenmarkt tunnel, and the bridges over the Oudegracht, ending at Buurkerkhof, illuminated by Gabriel Lester. Download the map before setting out and take your time.

Head downstairs for dinner in a werfkelder on the Oudegracht, one of the vaulted cellars beneath the street that have become cafés and restaurants. In the 19th century, some even served as homes; the tourist office recommends their indoor dining rooms in winter and tables on the wharves in summer. Reserve, especially on weekends, and request a table by the water if the weather allows.

visits.text: At the Drielandenpunt, you can put one foot in the Netherlands, the other in Belgium, and reach a hand toward Germany. This point, where the three countries meet, is on the Vaalserberg above Vaals. At 322.4 m, this summit is the highest point in the European part of the Netherlands. Until 1919, a fourth territory also touched this point: Neutral Moresnet, a tiny territory that has since become part of Belgium. On the Belgian side, you can climb the stairs or take the elevator up the 50 m Boudewijntoren. Parking costs €3 per car.

activities.text: The Labyrint Drielandenpunt combines hedges with walls of spraying water. The fastest visitors take up to 45 minutes to reach its center, where the Amikejo Turo tower, opened in 2024, stands. Its name means “the friendly tower” in Esperanto, the language some wanted Neutral Moresnet to adopt. Inside, a scale model brought to life by projections tells the story of this tiny territory, and the top floor offers views of the surrounding area. Expect to pay €9.50 per adult.

days_plan.itin_title: South Limburg in 4 Days: Maastricht, Valkenburg, Thorn

visits.text: Valkenburg’s Kasteelruïne is the only castle in the Netherlands built on a hill. Stadtholder William III, leader of the United Provinces, had it dismantled on December 10, 1672, to keep it from falling into French hands. Beneath the ruins, the guided tour of the Fluweelengrot follows 800 m of passages dug to extract stone for the castle. It passes through a secret chapel dating from 1797, where Mass was celebrated in secret during the French occupation. The temperature is 12 °C: bring a jacket.

Next, follow the Geul, the river that runs through Valkenburg, to the two surviving medieval gates, the Grendelpoort and the Berkelpoort. Many houses in the center are built of marl, a soft limestone quarried from the hills. As early as the 19th century, the small town became a popular vacation destination for wealthy Dutch visitors. Allow 30 minutes for a leisurely stroll between the two gates.

activities.text: If you are traveling with children, tour the Gemeentegrot on a small train: the ride lasts about 30 minutes, compared with 1 hour on foot. This former marl quarry, at the foot of the Cauberg hill, sheltered local residents during World War II. Families taking refuge carved their names into the walls beside the saw marks left by stonemasons. Fossil bones of a mosasaur, a marine reptile measuring 12 to 16 m, were also found here. The temperature underground is 12 °C.

Twelve percent: that is the maximum grade of the Cauberg, the 1.2 km climb starting in central Valkenburg. Riders in the Amstel Gold Race, a major Dutch cycling race, still climb it several times in each edition. The Road World Championships have used it five times, most recently in 2012. Walk up to get a sense of the effort, then head back down toward the entrance to the Gemeentegrot.

visits.text: Trade with Scotland left Veere with houses rather than just archives: the Schotse Huizen house part of Museum Veere. The visit continues at the Stadhuis on the Markt. Keep the same ticket for both locations; it covers both buildings, whose upper floors have no elevator access.

Enormous for such a small town, Veere’s Grote Kerk was nevertheless never completed. Projections and stories now bring new life to its nave. In spring and fall, the church generally opens Thursday through Sunday; the tower may close late in the season to protect the bats that hibernate there. Check opening hours before climbing.

visits.text: To understand what passes offshore, the Maritiem Muzeeum Zeeland is worth a stop in Vlissingen. Objects recovered from shipwrecks tell the story of life aboard, including bottles that still contain their wine. Pick up the audio guide included with admission and leave large bags in the coatroom; unlike the rest of the museum, the historic tower is not wheelchair accessible.

activities.text: Walk along Boulevard De Ruyter in Vlissingen to watch ships head into the estuary. Cargo ships pass close enough to shore to give the outdoor seating areas the feel of observation posts. Continue on foot toward Boulevard Bankert; avoid trying to drive through, as traffic is restricted during the season.
