visits.text: With 11.5 million cigar bands, the Volendams Museum turns tiny pieces of paper into monumental decorations. The Sigarenbandjeshuisje depicts the Leaning Tower of Pisa and St. Peter’s Basilica, among other landmarks; costumes and interior scenes place this curiosity in the context of local life. Locate this room at reception so you can leave enough time for it.

activities.text: You’ll follow Haven in Volendam to get a sense of the harbor before looking for a table. The boats face the waterfront shops; after the museum interiors, this walk reveals another side of the village. Opt for a short walking loop and compare menus before sitting down.

visits.text: Eight castles along 34 km: it sounds too good to be true—yet that is the reality of the cycling loop around Vorden, signposted since 1913. Most are private residences closed to the public, which makes them all the more fascinating. Kasteel Vorden, visible from the main road, is open six days a week with a freely accessible audio guide.

Kasteel Hackfort: its underground passage dating from the 14th century is one of the few parts open to the public, two afternoons a week. The historic kitchen garden, dating back to around 1790, is a must-see for garden lovers. The brasserie in the coach house cooks with vegetables from the garden. The first mention of Hackfort in the archives dates from 1392.

activities.text: Rent a bike in the village for the Achtkastelenroute, marked with yellow hexagonal signs from Vorden market square. The 34 km on paved roads pass Hackfort, Den Bramel, De Wildenborch and five other castles. A guided version is offered Wednesdays and Saturdays in summer.

visits.text: Raw concrete, soft light: at Deltawerk//, in the heart of the Waterloopbos, the walls of the former Deltagoot filter daylight like the slats of a giant blind. This channel generated full-scale waves to test the Delta Works structures. In 2018, RAAAF and Atelier de Lyon cut 80 cm thick slabs and rotated them 90 degrees along a 250 m stretch standing 7 m high. Free access from sunrise to sunset.

activities.text: Beneath its moss, the Waterloopbos conceals more than thirty hydraulic scale models from the former De Voorst laboratory, which operated here from 1951 to 1996. The ports of IJmuiden, Bangkok, and Lagos were tested here in miniature, without pumps: the low-lying terrain alone kept the water flowing. Designated a national monument in 2016, the woods take about 2 hours to explore. In fall, thousands of mushrooms appear: bring boots.

days_plan.itin_title: Flevoland in 3 Days: Polders, Marker Wadden, and Urk

visits.text: Nothing tells Terschelling’s story better than Museum ’t Behouden Huys, housed in whaling captains’ homes built in 1688. Follow Willem Barentsz to Novaya Zemlya, see two original nails and a chest key said to have survived 275 polar winters, then relive the fire of 1666 and the wreck of the Lutine. The museum opens in the afternoon, from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m., on selected days only: check before visiting.

Islanders simply call it “de toer,” the tower. Completed in 1594, the Brandaris is the oldest lighthouse in the Netherlands still in service, and its keepers monitor shipping traffic throughout the Wadden Sea day and night. It is closed to visitors: admire it from nearby Commandeurstraat, lined with 17th-century captains’ houses with stepped gables.

If it rains, head to the Centrum voor Natuur en Landschap, West-Terschelling’s nature museum. A saltwater fish aquarium, a touch pool where you can stroke rays, and a theater showing films about the Wadden on a loop all set the scene for the next day’s bike ride. Another room explains the island’s weather, useful before heading out into the wind. Outside peak season, opening days are limited: check before visiting.

Climb the Seinpaalduin near Willem Barentszkade: at 31.4 m, this dune is Terschelling’s highest point. It takes its name from a former signal mast whose colored lights indicated wind strength to ships in the Wadden. On a clear day, you can see as far as Vlieland; several paths lead up, some with steps.

In 1840, a barrel of cranberries washed ashore on Terschelling; the islanders planted the berries, which now cover 48 hectares. The Bessenschuur, a barn nestled in the forest on the Badweg toward West aan Zee, was used to sort the harvest and bills itself as Europe’s only original berry barn. It houses a tearoom and a bird exhibition, open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Gray concrete and silence: at the Bunkermuseum Terschelling, east of West-Terschelling, the Tigerstellung tells the story of the air war over the Wadden. This former German radar station from World War II retains several restored bunkers, and the visitor center explains the site through scale models and a film. Admission without a guided tour costs €5; book the 2-hour guided tour, limited to 16 people, well in advance.

activities.text: The wet sand of the Noordsvaarder reflects the evening light like a mirror at the island’s western tip. This sandbank joined Terschelling in the 19th century; part of it remained an air force training ground until 1996, and today you can spot avocets and harriers here. Walk from West-Terschelling toward the Groene Strand for sunset.

Board the Elixir, I Like Terschelling’s inflatable boat, at the floating dock in West-Terschelling’s harbor. In about 45 minutes, it speeds out to the sandbanks between Terschelling and Vlieland, in the heart of the Wadden Sea, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2009, where seals rest and often approach the boat. Life jackets and rain gear are provided, but bring a jacket: it’s cooler out on the water.

visits.text: Over 100,000 Jews, Sinti, and Roma were deported from Kamp Westerbork between 1942 and 1945 to Auschwitz, Sobibor, Theresienstadt, and Bergen-Belsen. Only 5,000 returned. The Herinneringscentrum Kamp Westerbork places personal stories at the center of its exhibition design: farewell letters, children's drawings, survivor testimonies. Entry €13.50.

The 102,000 stones on the former roll-call square each represent a deported victim who never returned. The twisted-rail monument, designed by survivor Ralph Prins, symbolizes transport that came to a halt. The camp site lies 3 km from the museum; the commandant's house dating from 1939, protected under a glass canopy, is the only original building.

activities.text: Walk to the camp grounds, 3 km from the museum, to see reconstructed barracks and monuments in their original locations. The audio tour (included in admission) lets you hear the voices of former prisoners. A free outdoor guided tour is offered some weekends.

visits.text: If you are looking for a lighthouse by the water, Westkapelle’s Hoge Licht will surprise you: it stands on the village side. This former church tower still guides boats. Choose a clear day for the climb; access to the panoramic view may be closed during storms or bad weather.

In 1944, bombing of the dike let the sea flood into Westkapelle; the Polderhuismuseum recounts the human consequences. Personal accounts and photographs connect this history to work on the dikes. Keep your phone handy for content accessed through QR codes, then view the coast through the lens of this story.

days_plan.itin_title: Zeeland in 4 Days: Harbors, Beaches, and the Dike Route

visits.text: You’ll start at the Mauritshuis in Willemstad, commissioned in 1623 by William of Orange’s son. A hunting lodge, governor’s residence, military hospital, military police barracks, then town hall: this house has seen it all. Since 2021, it has housed the visitor center and a local history museum. Free admission; closed Mondays.

Here, the pulpit takes the altar’s place at the center: Willemstad’s Koepelkerk has an octagonal layout designed around the sermon. Completed in 1607, it is considered the first church in the Netherlands designed from the outset for Protestant worship. You can visit in summer, particularly from July to September, according to locally published opening hours; check before coming. The tower is accessible during some of these opening hours.

activities.text: Wind sweeps Willemstad’s ramparts, which William the Silent had fortified in 1583; the seven bastions still form an almost intact star. Follow the rampart walkway to d’Orangemolen, a grain mill dating from 1734 whose sails began turning again in 2004 after some forty years at a standstill, then head down toward the harbor and the Arsenaal.

days_plan.itin_title: Western Brabant in 3 Days: Breda, Biesbosch and Heusden

visits.text: The Jopie Huisman Museum is dedicated to Frisian painter Jopie Huisman (1922–2000), who knew how to find value in humble or discarded objects. In the Golle, the museum café, objects from his home and barn are on display, including his red shirt and milking pants. Open daily from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.; admission €12.50, free for ages 12 and under, card payments only.

Twelve painted funeral biers line the side aisles of the Sint-Gertrudiskerk on Merk: nine belonged to guilds, and one was reserved for drowning victims, people who died by suicide, and prostitutes. The tourist office describes it as Friesland’s largest cruciform Late Gothic church, with the largest windows in the province. Look for the rood screen from 1569, then the oldest guild bier, dated 1666.

If boatmen’s stories appeal to you, head up to the attic of Museum Warkums Erfskip, housed in the Waag on Merk: there you can read old letters from boat captain Huijte Fookles. The floors feature models and accounts of Workum’s history, a town linked to Bolsward by a waterway dug in 1620. Allow 30 minutes, then take a look at the former town hall on the same square.

activities.text: Behind the large church, you’ll view Workum through a heart of water formed by the lions from its coat of arms, reimagined with Cornelia Parker’s British humor. Then head to Noard, where merchants’ houses once lined the Wymerts: the Sleeswijckhuis, at number 5, combines a stepped gable with a pilastered gable.

days_plan.itin_title: Eleven Cities of Friesland in 5 Days, Along the Elfsteden Route

visits.text: Burned in 1573 by the Beggars, rebels opposed to Spanish rule, Woudrichem was rebuilt around 1600. Hoogstraat, its main street, retains a series of gabled facades from that period. Look for the house called In den Gulden Engel, dated 1593. On Kerkstraat, the Gevangenpoort, the “prison gate,” was rebuilt after the fire. It served as a courthouse for many years. Allow 45 minutes for these two streets.

activities.text: Park in Woudrichem and follow the ramparts on foot. Their bastions and ravelins, pointed defensive outworks, were part of the water defense lines. The principle was simple: deliberately flood the land to stop the enemy. Then walk along the old harbor to the landing for the pedestrian and bicycle ferry, which crosses to Slot Loevestein. There is no fixed schedule: ring the bell and the ferryman will come and get you.

days_plan.itin_title: Rivierenland in 3 Days: Nijmegen, Loevestein, Gorinchem

visits.text: Yerseke’s oyster ponds look like small, tranquil pools, but they are part of an industry that is still very much alive. Connected to the Oosterschelde, they support the work of oyster farmers and follow the rhythm of the tides. Come at low tide: the ponds partially drain, revealing the oysters.

activities.text: Settle in at the Oesterij in Yerseke to compare the oysters on offer, overlooking the ponds and the Oosterschelde. The tasting may include oysters from different places: ask which come from Zeeland if you want to try locally produced oysters. Arrive before the lunchtime rush; the tasting counter does not take table reservations.

days_plan.itin_title: Zeeland in 4 Days: Harbors, Beaches, and the Dike Route

visits.text: Every half hour, the Gasthuistoren’s carillon plays a tune above Zaltbommel. A carillon is a set of tuned bells used to play melodies. This tower with its pear-shaped roof belonged to the town’s former hospital, the Groote Bommelsche Gasthuis. It was added about a century after the first buildings, which date from the 14th century. To hear a carillonneur play live, stop by on Tuesday morning or Friday evening.

Plain on the outside, Zaltbommel’s Sint-Maartenskerk conceals more than fifty medieval murals on its walls, vaults, and pillars. The Gothic church dates mainly from the 15th century. Its short, massive tower replaced a tall spire that had been struck by lightning several times. Admission is free. In October, the church is open Tuesday through Friday from 1:30 to 4 p.m., as well as Saturday from 11 a.m. and Sunday from 1 p.m. In November and December, it remains open Friday through Sunday; check the hours for the season. Tower tours take place on weekends at 2 p.m. and 3:15 p.m. (€5).

Stadskasteel Zaltbommel, literally “town castle,” is actually a large residence. It was commissioned in 1535 by Maarten van Rossem, captain of the armies of Gelderland, the province you are visiting. Today it houses Zaltbommel’s history museum. The exhibits tell the story of the town and this military leader’s role. The museum is open Tuesday through Sunday, from 1 to 5 p.m.: save it for the afternoon.

activities.text: End the day on Zaltbommel’s former ramparts, now gardens. Seven bastions, pointed projections from the rampart, were built here around 1600. Then follow Waterstraat down to the Waterpoort, the only one of the town’s five city gates still standing. It opens onto the Waalkade, the quay along the Waal. The road bridge that once crossed the river here, since replaced, inspired Dutch poet Martinus Nijhoff’s sonnet “De moeder de vrouw” (“The Mother, the Woman”).

days_plan.itin_title: Rivierenland in 3 Days: Nijmegen, Loevestein, Gorinchem

visits.text: Known as the “Dikke Toren,” or “fat tower,” the Sint-Lievensmonstertoren is Zierikzee’s most recognizable landmark. Its panoramic view unfolds 62 meters above the city. Arrive at least one hour before closing to make the climb; the ground-floor exhibition is free to visit.

Follow Zierikzee’s quays to the Zuidhavenpoort and Noordhavenpoort. These medieval gates protected access from the harbor; between them, a bascule bridge spans the old harbor entrance. Continue your walk along the Nieuwe Haven to see the historic boats.

days_plan.itin_title: Zeeland in 4 Days: Harbors, Beaches, and the Dike Route

visits.text: The people of Zutphen chained their books in the 16th century for an indisputable reason: theft. The Librije at the Sint Walburgiskerk, built between 1561 and 1564, is the only chained library in the Netherlands still in its original condition. The collection contains around 750 volumes, including first editions of Copernicus and Erasmus. Visits are guided only, throughout the opening day.

Sint Walburgiskerk dates from the 11th century in its oldest parts. It houses a ring-shaped candle chandelier from 1395, a copper holy-water font from 1527 and the Hendrick Bader organ of 1643, restored to its original condition in 1996. The tower can be climbed at weekends and during school holidays, for an unobstructed view over Zutphen and the IJssel. Church entry €10, tower an additional €5.

Looking down over the IJssel from the top of the Walburgiskerk tower is the reward for climbing more than 200 steps. Zutphen, a former Hanseatic city whose golden age stretched from the 13th to the 16th century, retains a compact historic centre with merchant façades fronting buildings that are still inhabited. The Hof van Heeckeren, a 17th-century town palace opposite the Walburgiskerk, houses two museums under one roof.

activities.text: If you appreciate craft beer, the Stadsbrouwerij Cambrinus on the Houtmarkt has brewed its own beers since 2006, in a room with copper brewing vats visible from the tables. The café also offers a selection of Dutch speciality beers. Count on an hour in the evening after sightseeing.

Stroll along the Berkelkade beside the River Berkel, which joins the IJssel at Zutphen: Hanseatic warehouses converted into flats and restaurants line the quay. It's the most photographed stretch in town, especially in the evening when the façades are reflected in the water.

days_plan.itin_title: Eastern Netherlands - Hanseatic League, Veluwe and Achterhoek in 10 Days

visits.text: Built in 1409, two years after Zwolle joined the Hanseatic League, the Sassenpoort is the sole surviving city gate from the old ramparts. Its 101,000 trachyte and sandstone blocks bear witness to the commercial wealth of the era. It's open Wednesdays and Saturdays from 11 AM to 5 PM, entrance €3, and features a permanent Hanseatic hall accessed via the medieval staircase.

Touristy but well done: Zwolle's Grote Markt is ringed by 16th-century merchant façades and a café terrace tucked into the Wijndragerstoren tower. A stone's throw away, Sint-Michaelskerk displays a statue of the archangel on its roof—there's a green version in the square, look for it. Saturday's open-air market remains one of the liveliest in Overijssel.

The scent of old paper and waxed wood greets you at Van der Velde in de Broeren, a bookshop housed since 2013 in a neo-Gothic church dating from 1901. The shelves climb all the way to the vaults, and a café occupies the chancel. An hour easily slips away. Avoid Sunday mornings, when it gets crowded.

Museum de Fundatie is worth a stop on the way back: its egg-shaped roof—nicknamed “De Wolk”—is clad in 55,000 white-and-blue ceramic tiles from Makkum, added in 2012–2013 to the 19th-century neoclassical building. The collection includes Mondrians and Van Goghs, and temporary exhibitions change constantly.

Stop at Zwolle's Grote Markt square for one last coffee on a terrace before hitting the road. The square is bordered by 15th- and 16th-century merchant façades, with Sint-Michaelskerk closing off the view at the far end. Saturday's market is one of the largest in Overijssel, with several hundred stalls depending on the season.

activities.text: Take the trail around the star-shaped ramparts surrounding the historic centre: the outline of the old fortifications is still visible in the canal layout. The 2.4-km walk, signposted by the tourist office, passes beneath the Sassenpoort and alongside several towers still standing.

If the sun cooperates, climb the 236 steps of the Peperbus to the first landing at 51 metres: the tower of the Onze-Lieve-Vrouwebasiliek soars to 75 metres but public access stops there, and the view over the polders and the IJssel is already clear. Check opening hours at the basilica before coming.

If it's a Wednesday or Saturday, the Sassenpoort is open from 11 am to 5 pm for €3: a quick visit to the Hanseatic hall inside the gate is a fitting way to end the journey exploring the Hanseatic League. From the gate's opening in 1409 to today's return, the Dutch Hanseatic circuit comes full circle.
